z-index: -1;\n  position: absolute;\n  content: '';\n  bottom: 35px;\n  left: 10px;\n  width: 50%;\n  top: 80%;\n  max-width: 300px;\n  background: #777;\n  box-shadow: 0 35px 20px #777;\n  transform: background: #fdfdfd;\n  margin: 2rem;\n  line-height: 1.5;\n  position: relative;\n  box-shadow:\n    0 4px 0 -2px #ddd,\n    1px 1px 0 0 #f7f7f7;\n}\n\n.data-card:before,\n.data-card:after {\n  z-index: -1;\n  position: absolute;\n  content: '';\n  bottom: 35px;\n  left: 10px;\n  width: 50%;\n  top: 80%;\n  max-width: 300px;\n  background: #777;\n  box-shadow: 0 35px 20px #777;\n  transform: rotate(-4deg);\n}\n\n.data-card::after {\n  transform: rotate(4deg);\n  right: 10px;\n  left: auto;\n}\n\n.data-card\u003e* {\n  padding: 0.6rem 1.2rem;\n}\n\n.data-card h1 {\n  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 4.2vw, 3rem);\n  line-height: 1;\n  font-weight: 500;\n}\n\n.data-card .name {\n  grid-column: 1/-1;\n  grid-row: 2;\n  padding-bottom: 1.2rem;\n}\n\n.data-card .info,\n.data-card .location,\n.data-card .type,\n.data-card .pattern {\n  grid-column: 1 / span 2;\n}\n\n.data-card .date,\n.data-card .weight {\n  transform: rotate(180deg);\n  writing-mode: vertical-lr;\n  padding: 'bg-gradient-to-b from-neutral-900 to-stone-900 dark:from-stone-700 dark:to-neutral-800/80'\n          : ''\n      )}\n      layoutRoot\n      layout\n      initial={{ borderRadius: 21, width: '4rem', height: '4rem' }}\n      animate={\n        isExpanded\n          ? {\n            borderRadius: 20,\n            width: CONTAINER_SIZE,\n            height: CONTAINER_SIZE + 50,\n\n            transition: {\n              type: 'spring',\n              damping: 25,\n              stiffness: 400,\n              when: 'beforeChildren',\n            },\n          }\n          : {\n            borderRadius: 21,\n            width: '4rem',\n            height: '4rem',\n          }\n      }\n    \u003e\n      {children}",

        "contents": "\"use client\";\n\nimport { cn } from \"@/utils\";\nimport { useTheme } from \"next-themes\";\nimport { useEffect, useState } from \"react\";\n\n/**\n * ThemeSwitcher component that provides a sidebar UI for switching between light, dark, custom, and system themes\n */\nexport const ThemeSwitcher = () =\u003e {\n\tconst { theme, setTheme } = useTheme();\n\tconst [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false);\n\n\t// Wait for component to be mounted to avoid hydration mismatch\n\tuseEffect(() =\u003e {\n\t\tsetMounted(true);\n\t}, []);\n\n\tif (!mounted) return null;\n\n\treturn (\n\t\t\u003cdiv className=\"absolute bottom-10 flex left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-8 md:fixed md:top-1/2 md:bottom-auto md:left-4 md:flex-col md:translate-x-0 gap-2 md:-translate-y-1/2 bg-gray-100 border-gray-95 border-solid border p-2 rounded z-40 shadow-super\"\u003e\n\t\t\t\u003cThemeButton\n\t\t\t\ttooltip=\"Light\"\n\t\t\t\tisSelected={theme === \"light\"}\n\t\t\t\tonClick={() =\u003e setTheme(\"light\")}\n\t\t\t\tariaLabel=\"Switch to light theme\"\n\t\t\t\u003e",

        "originalContents": "\"use client\";\n\nimport { cn } from \"@/utils\";\nimport { useTheme } from \"next-themes\";\nimport { useEffect, useState } from \"react\";\n\n/**\n * ThemeSwitcher component that provides a sidebar UI for switching between light, dark, custom, and system themes\n */\nexport const ThemeSwitcher = () =\u003e {\n\tconst { theme, setTheme } = useTheme();\n\tconst [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false);\n\n\t// Wait for component to be mounted to avoid hydration mismatch\n\tuseEffect(() =\u003e {\n\t\tsetMounted(true);\n\t}, []);\n\n\tif (!mounted) return null;\n\n\treturn (\n\t\t\u003cdiv className=\"absolute bottom-10 flex left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-8 md:fixed md:top-1/2 md:bottom-auto md:left-4 md:flex-col md:translate-x-0 gap-2 md:-translate-y-1/2 bg-gray-100 border-gray-95 border-solid border p-2 rounded z-40 shadow-super\"\u003e\n\t\t\t\u003cThemeButton\n\t\t\t\ttooltip=\"Light\"\n\t\t\t\tisSelected={theme === \"light\"}\n\t\t\t\tonClick={() =\u003e setTheme(\"light\")}\n\t\t\t\tariaLabel=\"Switch to light theme\"\n\t\t\t\u003e",

Whether you’re prototyping UI components or optimizing for accessibility, this guide will equip you with a deep understanding of what it means to design in the Liquid era.\n\n## Introduction\n\n**During WWDC 2025**, Apple launched Liquid Glass—a fully integrated, cross-platform design language now embedded into **iOS 26**, **macOS 26**, **iPadOS 26**, **watchOS 26**, and **tvOS 26**.\n\nUnlike traditional visual updates, Liquid Glass update represents a paradigm shift in how interfaces behave and respond to user interaction. By blending real-time light manipulation, spatial depth, and motion-driven feedback, Apple has established a new blueprint for building intuitive and aesthetically rich user interfaces.\n\nThe system adapts to touch, device orientation, content, and accessibility preferences—all while maintaining visual harmony and usability. For today’s UX and UI designers, Liquid Glass presents a highly flexible yet demanding material that rewards thoughtful, user-centric execution.\n\n\u003e Apple's design systems: Aqua, iOS 7, visionOS\n\n## What is Liquid Glass?\n\nLiquid Glass is Apple’s first truly dynamic UI material, combining visual style and behavior into a unified system. Unlike static gradients or flat blurs, it is **fully responsive**. It's bending light in real time to create fluid layers, nuanced depth, and environmental adaptation.\n\nThe material uses **lensing**, a technique that bends and concentrates light to help users intuitively understand what belongs where in the interface. Rather than mimicking physical glass, it simulates its properties in a digitally native way—producing lightweight, interactive layers that adjust continuously in form and behavior.\n\n## Core UX principles behind Liquid Glass\n\nAt its core, Liquid Glass communicates visually through **light, shadow, and motion**. Navigation bars flex, shift, and subtly animate; buttons glow upon touch, and elements organically lift into view or recede into rest states.\n\nEach layer behaves with **contextual awareness**, ensuring the user always knows where to focus. Transparency allows interface elements to float above content while **preserving legibility** through contrast and shadow play. These visual dynamics are paired with strong accessibility support—allowing system toggles to gracefully override animations or transparency without disrupting the design intent.\n\n## Introduction\n\n**During WWDC 2025**, Apple launched Liquid Glass—a fully integrated, cross-platform design language now embedded into **iOS 26**, **macOS 26**, **iPadOS 26**, **watchOS 26**, and **tvOS 26**.\n\nUnlike traditional visual updates, Liquid Glass update represents a paradigm shift in how interfaces behave and respond to user interaction. By blending real-time light manipulation, spatial depth, and motion-driven feedback, Apple has established a new blueprint for building intuitive and aesthetically rich user interfaces.\n\nThe system adapts to touch, device orientation, content, and accessibility preferences—all while maintaining visual harmony and usability. For today’s UX and UI designers, Liquid Glass presents a highly flexible yet demanding material that rewards thoughtful, user-centric execution.\n\n\u003e Apple's design systems: Aqua, iOS 7, visionOS\n\n## What is Liquid Glass?\n\nLiquid Glass is Apple’s first truly dynamic UI material, combining visual style and behavior into a unified system. Unlike static gradients or flat blurs, it is **fully responsive**. It's bending light in real time to create fluid layers, nuanced depth, and environmental adaptation.\n\nThe material uses **lensing**, a technique that bends and concentrates light to help users intuitively understand what belongs where in the interface. Rather than mimicking physical glass, it simulates its properties in a digitally native way—producing lightweight, interactive layers that adjust continuously in form and behavior.\n\n## Core UX principles behind Liquid Glass\n\nAt its core, Liquid Glass communicates visually through **light, shadow, and motion**. Navigation bars flex, shift, and subtly animate; buttons glow upon touch, and elements organically lift into view or recede into rest states.\n\nEach layer behaves with **contextual awareness**, ensuring the user always knows where to focus. Transparency allows interface elements to float above content while **preserving legibility** through contrast and shadow play. These visual dynamics are paired with strong accessibility support—allowing system toggles to gracefully override animations or transparency without disrupting the design intent.\n\n## Platform highlights: Liquid Glass in action\n\nApple’s Liquid Glass design adapts to each platform while maintaining a unified visual and behavioral system. Each device presents unique interaction patterns and display contexts, and Liquid Glass adjusts accordingly—ensuring both consistency and contextual optimization.\n\n### iOS 26\n\n* The tab bar dynamically shrinks during scroll and expands when interaction resumes, maintaining user focus.\n* Lock Screen numerals wrap behind user photos using intelligent lensing for seamless integration.\n* Icons and widgets use layered glass effects that react to wallpaper and tint.\n\n### iPadOS 26\n\n* Navigation evolves into floating sidebars, replacing bottom tab bars on larger screens.\n* Sidebars dynamically reflect surrounding color and content, enhancing spatial awareness.\n* Visual consistency with macOS strengthens multi-device fluency.\n\n### macOS 26\n\n* A transparent menu bar blends into the wallpaper, creating more open visual space.\n* Active windows appear crisp and bright, while inactive windows subtly fade via opacity.\n* Toolbars and sidebars behave as floating layers with refined shadow and depth.\n\n### watchOS 26\n\n* Notifications and overlays use high-contrast Liquid Glass panels for clarity.\n* Buttons glow subtly when tapped, enhancing responsiveness with minimal animation.\n* Visual consistency with iOS improves usability across devices.\n\n### tvOS 26\n\n* Menus and overlays use soft blur and refraction to sit comfortably over content.\n* Focused items glow internally, removing the need for hard outlines.\n\n## Accessibility enhancements across platforms\n\nAccessibility is a foundational element of Liquid Glass. The material **responds automatically** to user preferences—simplifying transitions under Reduce Motion, adding opacity when Reduce Transparency is enabled, and increasing separation when Increase Contrast is on.\n\nIt adjusts shadow opacity, blur density, and brightness dynamically depending on the underlying content. Additionally, **users can select appearance styles** that best suit their visual needs. However, real-world usage scenarios still require **thoughtful testing**, especially when overlapping layered content and dynamic backgrounds.\n\n## Design considerations and best practices\n\n* Use Liquid Glass for navigation and UI framing—not content layers.\n* Avoid stacking multiple glass layers, which can reduce clarity.\n* Use tinting to emphasize actions—but only sparingly.\n\nDesigning with Liquid Glass is a strategic exercise. You should apply the material where it reinforces structure—**navigation bars, tab bars, sidebars**—not on scrollable content areas. **Layering multiple glass components** **leads to clutter** and weakens visual hierarchy.\n\nRegular and Clear variants for Liquid Glass contrast\n\n\u003e The Regular variant is adaptable and works in almost all contexts, while Clear is better suited for surfaces sitting over media-rich content, provided you add enough contrast.\n\nTinting can enhance visibility or branding but must be used selectively to avoid disrupting balance\n\n\u003e Tinting can enhance visibility or branding but must be used selectively to avoid disrupting balance. Overall, design choices should support clarity, reinforce hierarchy, and respect individual user settings.\n\n#### Liquid Glass UI Kit for Sketch\n\nSketch has already released its **official UI library for macOS 26**. which is great news for teams getting an early start. They also announced that more updates are on the way, especially for designers currently working on app redesigns. We should expect a lot of beta updates over the summer! \n\n## Final thoughts: Our point of view\n\nLiquid Glass is **expressive, modern, and motion-rich**. It brings a sense of depth and tactility that makes digital interfaces feel more alive—more responsive to light, motion, and touch. Its cross-platform consistency is a clear win for design teams working across the **Apple ecosystem**.\n\nBut expressive doesn’t always mean accessible. Right now, it feels like there’s too much transparency with **not enough contrast**. In environments with busy backgrounds or **low contrast**, content clarity takes a hit—especially for users with visual impairments.\n\nWith better contrast handling and more thoughtful transparency defaults, Liquid Glass **has the potential to be both beautiful and truly inclusive.**\n\nWe’re thrilled to invite you to join our incredible community of product designers (and enthusiasts) by **following us on Instagram**.       "chunk": "Sitemap\n\nOpen in app\n\nSign up\n\nSign in\n\nMedium Logo\n\nWrite\n\nSign up\n\nSign in\n\nPixelmatters\n\n·\n\nPixelmatters\n\nDigital Product Studio. \u003chttps://pixelmatters.com\u003e\n\n# 8 UI design trends we’re seeing in 2025\n\nGabriela Rocha\n\nGabriela Rocha\n\n5 min read\n\n·\n\nMar 17, 2025\n\n\\--\n\n12\n\nListen\n\nShare\n\nLet’s be real — digital products aren’t built on trends. They evolve through iteration, feedback, and a lot of trial and error as we figure out what users need, what businesses want, and what’s feasible to build. But every year, certain UI and interaction patterns gain traction, shaping how users perceive and interact with digital products. So, **while trends shouldn’t dictate design decisions, they can offer useful insights into shifts in user expectations**.\n\nHere’s what’s emerging in 2025:\n\n# 1\\. Beyond flat design\n\nMinimalism isn’t just about clean lines and white space — it’s evolving to feel more dynamic and engaging. While simplicity still drives usability, designers are layering in subtle, intentional details to make interfaces feel more alive:\n\n* **Microinteractions** → Small but meaningful animations on components that add personality and feedback.\n* **Strategic color pops** → Bright accents that guide attention without overwhelming the user.\n* **Immersive 3D elements** → More brands incorporate 3D illustrations in product visuals, marketing assets, and digital branding.\n* **Expressive typography** → Custom typefaces are becoming a bigger investment, with brands like Discord embracing more playful fonts.\n\nMinimalism isn’t going away — it’s just becoming a little less predictable.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nDiscord Brand Refresh 2025\n\n# 2\\. Post-Neumorphism: depth with clarity\n\nNeumorphism looked great in Dribbble shots and design explorations, but in reality, it’s tough to maintain in a design system and time-consuming to develop. That said, “morphism” is making a subtle comeback — not as full interfaces but in small details like app icons, certain UI components in web and mobile apps (like buttons and menus), marketing websites, and more recently, in spatial design UI. The key now is balance: using shadows and bevels thoughtfully. As the **Polaris design system** puts it, _“Depth introduces a sense of realism, helps establish visual hierarchy, and creates focus.”_\n\n**The result? UI elements that feel tactile and engaging while staying functional and accessible.**\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nPolaris Design System: Shopify has introduced depth in its web app for certain UI components.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nApple’s spatial design UI incorporates glassmorphism effects.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nApple’s macOS and iOS have moved towards a more balanced approach to depth, using subtle shadows and layering while maintaining clear contrast for accessibility.\n\n# 3\\. Motion as feedback, not aesthetics\n\nMicro-interactions and motion design are more purposeful. Instead of flashy animations, movement should be about guiding users, improving usability, and providing instant feedback. Subtle hover states, smooth transitions, and responsive gestures make interfaces feel intuitive rather than overwhelming.\n\n# 4\\. Dark Mode\n\nDark mode isn’t just a nice-to-have anymore — it’s becoming the default in many apps. The focus now is on adaptive contrast, improved readability, and lighting adjustments based on time of day or system settings.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nCausal Web App — Dark Mode\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nLinear Web App — Dark Mode\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nNotion Web \u0026 Desktop App — Dark Mode\n\n# 5\\. Text-first Interfaces\n\nWith AI-generated summaries, chat-based interactions, and voice interfaces, text-first design is making a comeback. More products are prioritizing clear, digestible content over heavy visuals.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nRaycast: a Mac productivity tool where users interact through a text-based command interface rather than traditional UI navigation.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nHEY: a redesigned email experience that emphasizes structured, text-based interaction rather than cluttered inboxes with excessive visuals.\n\n# 6\\. Functional AI: more than just chatbots\n\nAI is everywhere, but not every integration works. Many products push AI before it’s ready, leading to half-baked features and overhyped launches (like failed AI hardware in 2024). Too often, “fail fast” means shipping AI that doesn’t actually help users.\n\nThe best AI makes things easier — smart recommendations, automated summaries, and real-time assistance that actually improves usability instead of adding friction.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nMicrosoft’s Seeing AI: helps visually impaired users by describing objects, reading text, and identifying people.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nPerplexity AI: AI-powered search engine.\n\n# 7\\. Ethical \u0026 sustainable UX\n\nUsers are more conscious of digital sustainability. Expect more low-energy UI designs, reduced unnecessary animations, and ethical design choices that reduce digital waste.\n\nA big factor is **performance** — slow, bloated websites and apps use more energy, from servers to user devices. The fix? **Smaller file sizes, better coding, and streamlined design** to keep things fast and efficient.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nWebsite Carbon Calculator: analyzes websites and provides feedback on how to reduce their environmental impact\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nEcosia (The Search Engine That Plants Trees): uses ad revenue to fund tree planting projects, helping offset the carbon impact of web searches.\n\n# 8\\. Offline-first experiences\n\nWith increased focus on accessibility and global reach, apps and websites are becoming more resilient. Features like offline access, progressive web apps, and smart caching ensure uninterrupted productivity.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nGoogle Maps Offline Mode: allows users to download maps and navigate without an internet connection, making travel more accessible in low-connectivity areas.\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\nFigma’s offline mode: allows users to keep working on designs even without an internet connection, syncing changes once they’re back online.\n\n# Final thoughts\n\nTrends come and go, but good design remains focused on usability, accessibility, and solving real problems. In 2025 and onward, digital products won’t just look good — they’ll work better, adapt intelligently, and work better to respect the user’s time and attention.\n\nSo, take trends with a grain of salt, but pay attention to what actually improves experiences on the context of your product. That’s where real design impact happens.\n\nDesign Trends\n\nUI\n\nDesign\n\nUser Interface\n\nUI Design\n\n\\--\n\n\\--\n\n12\n\nPixelmatters\n\nPixelmatters\n\nPublished in Pixelmatters\n\n678 followers\n\n·Last published Apr 17, 2025\n\nDigital Product Studio. \u003chttps://pixelmatters.com\u003e\n\nGabriela Rocha\n\nGabriela Rocha\n\nWritten by Gabriela Rocha\n\n64 followers\n\n·51 following\n\nDigital Product Designer\n\n## Responses (12)\n\nSee all responses\n\nHelp\n\nStatus\n\nAbout\n\nCareers\n\nPress\n\nBlog\n\nPrivacy\n\nRules\n\nTerms\n\nText to speech",

Report Abuse \n\nCover image for WWDC 2025: Apple's Liquid Glass Design System \n\nArshTechPro \n\nArshTechPro \n\n Posted on Jun 24 \n\n#  WWDC 2025: Apple's Liquid Glass Design System\n\n#ios #mobile #designsystem #ux \n\nApple has unveiled its most extensive software design update with **Liquid Glass**, fundamentally reshaping how interfaces interact with content. This comprehensive guide breaks down the key changes every iOS developer needs to implement.\n\n##  The Foundation: Liquid Glass Principles\n\n###  Core Philosophy\n\n* **Harmonized design language** across all Apple platforms\n* **Cohesive, adaptive, and expressive** interface elements\n* **Shared design foundation** leveraging SwiftUI, Mac Catalyst, and iPad Window Resizing\n* **Systematic approach** considering every element from smallest control to largest surface\n\n###  Visual Design Updates\n\n####  System Colors\n\n* Adjusted across Light, Dark, and Increased Contrast appearances\n* Enhanced hue differentiation while maintaining Apple's optimistic spirit\n* Optimized for harmony with Liquid Glass materials\n\n####  Typography Refinements\n\n* **Bolder text rendering** for improved clarity\n* **Left-aligned typography** in critical moments (alerts, onboarding)\n* Strengthened structure and readability\n\n##  Shape System Architecture\n\n###  Three Core Shape Types\n\n####  1\\. Fixed Shapes\n\n* Constant corner radius regardless of container size\n* Predictable geometry for consistent layouts\n\n####  2\\. Capsules\n\n* Radius equals half the container height\n* Natural concentricity support\n* Primary choice for touch-friendly interfaces\n* **Platform Usage:**  \n   * iOS/iPadOS: Preferred for most interactive elements  \n   * macOS: Reserved for Large and X-Large controls, standout actions\n\n####  3\\. Concentric Shapes\n\n* Radius calculated by subtracting padding from parent container\n* Automatic inner radii calculation for nested elements\n* **Pro Tip:** Use &#96;concentricShape&#96; with fallback radius for components that work both nested and standalone\n\n###  Platform-Specific Implementation\n\n####  iOS/iPadOS\n\n* Capsules dominate the interface\n* Mirrored proportions in sliders, switches, bars, and buttons\n* Grouped table view corners follow capsule geometry\n\n####  macOS\n\n* Mini, Small, Medium controls: Rounded rectangles\n* Large controls: Capsule shapes\n* New X-Large size leverages Liquid Glass for spacious layouts\n* Creates hierarchy in complex desktop environments\n\n###  Design System Harmony\n\n####  Critical Considerations\n\n* Interface elements must complement system rhythm, not clash\n* Avoid corners that feel \"pinched\" or \"flared\"\n* Nested containers require concentric alignment\n* **Device Edge Handling:**  \n   * Phone: Capsules with extra margin near screen edges  \n   * iPad/Mac: Concentric shapes aligned with window edges\n\n##  Functional Layer Architecture\n\n###  Liquid Glass as UI Layer\n\n* Floats above content providing structure without stealing focus\n* Creates spatial relationships between surfaces\n* Maintains connection to interaction sources\n\n###  Navigation and Focus\n\n####  Action Sheets Evolution\n\n* **Before:** Always appeared at screen bottom\n* **Now:** Springs directly from triggering action\n* Clearly defined source-to-surface relationships\n\n####  Material Application\n\n* Apply materials directly to controls, not inner views\n* Supports spatial interaction understanding\n\n###  Focus Management\n\n####  Modal vs Parallel Tasks\n\n* **Modal interruptions:** Liquid Glass + dimming layer for centered attention\n* **Parallel tasks:** Natural separation without flow disruption\n* **Focus shifts:** Material becomes more opaque and larger during deep engagement\n\n##  Navigation Structure Updates\n\n###  Bar Components\n\n####  Customization Cleanup\n\n* Remove unnecessary backgrounds and borders\n* System appearance eliminates need for manual emphasis\n* Hierarchy expressed through layout and grouping, not decoration\n\n####  Grouping Best Practices\n\n* Items grouped via correct API automatically share backgrounds\n* **Function and frequency grouping** for related actions\n* Avoid mixing symbols with text (perceived as single button)\n* Primary actions (Done) remain separate with blue tint (iOS/iPadOS) or prominent text (macOS)\n\n###  Tab Bar Optimization\n\n* **New dedicated Search tab** on iOS for improved accessibility\n* Support for persistent features via accessory views (media controls)\n* Avoid screen-specific actions (checkout buttons belong with content)\n* Clear separation between persistent and contextual elements\n\n##  Visual Effects System\n\n###  Content Separation Requirements\n\n* Liquid Glass elements require clear content separation for legibility\n* Controls sit on system materials, never directly on content\n* Maintains contrast and visual hierarchy\n\n###  Scroll Edge Effects\n\n####  Two Distinct Styles\n\n* **Soft (Default):** Subtle transitions for iOS/iPadOS interactive elements\n* **Hard (macOS):** Stronger boundaries for text controls and pinned headers\n* **Never mix or stack** different edge effect styles\n\n####  Implementation Rules\n\n* One scroll edge effect per view\n* Split View layouts: Each pane maintains consistent height alignment\n* Not decorative—only used where floating UI elements exist\n\n###  Sidebar Enhancements\n\n* Now inset and built with Liquid Glass\n* Content extends to edge for immersive experience\n* **Background extension effects** for hero images and tinted backgrounds\n* Scroll views extend beneath sidebar by default\n* Per-view background extension flexibility\n\n##  Cross-Platform Continuity\n\n###  Device Context Understanding\n\n* **iPhone:** Narrow, vertical, zoomed-in focus\n* **iPad:** Bridge between iPhone utility and Mac expansiveness\n* **Mac:** Wide, expansive canvas with full depth\n\n###  Design Once, Deploy Everywhere\n\n* Single anatomy design for all platforms\n* Platform variations as expressions, not exceptions\n* Consistent component behavior across devices\n\n###  Symbol and Content Strategy\n\n####  Symbol Usage\n\n* Same symbols across devices preserve meaning\n* Bars increasingly rely on symbols over text\n* Menus populated with symbols for recognition\n* **Related actions:** Single symbol for group introduction, text for specifics\n\n####  Component Anatomy\n\n* Shared structural elements across platforms\n* Consistent placement of selection indicators, icons, labels, accessories\n* **Behavior consistency:** Same core interactions regardless of platform form factor\n\n##  Few Implementation Checklist\n\n###  Immediate Actions\n\n* \\[ \\] Update custom bar implementations (remove extra backgrounds/borders)\n* \\[ \\] Audit nested container corner radii for concentricity\n* \\[ \\] Implement proper grouping APIs for bar items\n* \\[ \\] Review tab bar organization and add Search tab if applicable\n* \\[ \\] Apply correct scroll edge effects (soft vs hard)\n\n###  Design System Updates\n\n* \\[ \\] Align custom components with three shape types\n* \\[ \\] Implement concentric shape calculations\n* \\[ \\] Update color usage for Liquid Glass harmony\n* \\[ \\] Refine typography alignment (left-align critical text)\n* \\[ \\] Test component behavior across all target platforms\n\n##  Resources\n\nThe Human Interface Guidelines have been updated with comprehensive Liquid Glass documentation. It controls how child elements (grid items) are arranged.\n* **CSS Grid Item**: A child element of a grid container. It is placed within the grid and can span across rows or columns based on the grid's setup.\n\n| Grid Container Properties | Grid Item Properties |\n| ------------------------- | -------------------- |\n| display                   | grid-column-start    |\n| grid-template-columns     | grid-column-end      |\n| grid-template-rows        | grid-row-start       |\n| grid-template-areas       | grid-row-end         |\n| grid-template             | grid-column          |\n| grid-column-gap           | grid-row             |\n| grid-row-gap              | grid-area            |\n| grid-gap                  | justify-self         |\n| justify-items             | align-self           |\n| align-items               | place-self           |\n| place-items               | order                |\n| justify-content           | z-index              |\n| align-content             |                      |\n| place-content             |                      |\n| grid-auto-columns         |                      |\n| grid-auto-rows            |                      |\n| grid-auto-flow            |                      |\n| grid                      |                      |\n\n# CSS Flexbox\n\n* **CSS Flexbox Container**: The parent element that uses flexbox to control the layout of its child elements. It defines the flex behavior, such as direction, wrapping, and alignment.\n* **CSS Flexbox Item**: A direct child of a flexbox container that follows the container's flex layout.\n\n| Flexbox Container Properties | Flexbox Item Properties |\n| ---------------------------- | ----------------------- |\n| display                      | order                   |\n| flex-direction               | flex-grow               |\n| flex-wrap                    | flex-shrink             |\n| flex-flow                    | flex-basis              |\n| justify-content              | flex                    |\n| align-items                  | align-self              |\n| align-content                |                         |\n| gap                          |                         |\n| row-gap                      |                         |\n| column-gap                   |                         |\n\n---\n\nImportant\n\nIf you design with Tailwind, check out SERP Blocks \\- it's the largest component library built on Tailwind \u0026 Shadcn\n\n---\n\nserp-blocks\n\n---\n\n# Fundamental/Common Responsive Layouts for Websites/UIs\n\n1. How to Build Responsive Tables That ...\n\n# How to Build Responsive Tables That Don’t Break on Mobile: A Step-by-Step Guide with CSS Grid \u0026 Tailwind\n\nLearn how to create responsive tables using CSS Grid and Tailwind CSS that adapt perfectly for mobile devices without losing readability.\n\nWeb Development\n\nFeb 13, 2025\n\nHow to Build Responsive Tables That Don’t Break on Mobile: A Step-by-Step Guide with CSS Grid \u0026 Tailwind \n\n**Responsive tables are essential for mobile users, as over 60% of web traffic now comes from mobile devices.** Traditional tables often break on small screens, causing frustrating horizontal scrolling and poor readability. This guide shows you how to fix that using **CSS Grid** and **Tailwind CSS**.\n\n### Key Steps:\n\n* **Set Up Tailwind CSS:** Install and configure it for your project.\n* **Build a Semantic Table Structure:** Use accessible HTML with Tailwind utilities for responsive padding, spacing, and overflow handling.\n* **Use CSS Grid for Flexibility:** Create layouts that adapt to screen sizes, turning rows into card-like blocks for mobile.\n* **Mobile-First Design:** Stack table data vertically for small screens, then add columns back for larger devices with Tailwind’s breakpoints.\n* **Improve Usability:** Add ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, and lazy loading for better accessibility and performance.\n\n### Quick Comparison: CSS Grid vs. Tailwind CSS\n\nTailwind CSS\n\n| Feature           | CSS Grid Contribution        | Tailwind CSS Advantage          |\n| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------- |\n| Layout Control    | Dynamic column adjustments   | Pre-built responsive utilities  |\n| Mobile Adaptation | Stacking for small screens   | Mobile-first breakpoint system  |\n| Accessibility     | Preserves semantic structure | Built-in accessibility features |\n\n## Starting Your Project\n\nKicking off a responsive table project with Tailwind CSS involves setting up your development environment and building a solid HTML foundation. Here’s how to get started.\n\n### Setting Up Tailwind CSS\n\nFollow these steps to set up Tailwind CSS:\n\n1. Create a new project directory, initialize it with npm, and install Tailwind CSS:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmkdir build-components-using-tailwind\ncd build-components-using-tailwind\nnpm init -y\nnpm install tailwindcss\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Generate a Tailwind configuration file:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx tailwindcss init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Add the following lines to a &#96;tailwind.css&#96; file to include Tailwind’s core styles:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n@tailwind base;\n@tailwind components;\n@tailwind utilities;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Creating the Basic Table Structure\n\nStart by creating a semantic HTML structure for accessibility and easy styling:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"flow-root\"\u003e\n  \u003cdiv class=\"overflow-x-auto\"\u003e\n    \u003cdiv class=\"inline-block min-w-full py-2 align-middle sm:px-6 lg:px-8\"\u003e\n      \u003ctable class=\"min-w-full divide-y divide-base-300\"\u003e\n        \u003cthead\u003e\n          \u003ctr\u003e\n            \u003cth scope=\"col\" class=\"py-3.5 pl-4 pr-3 text-left text-sm font-medium text-base-500 sm:pl-0\"\u003eName\u003c/th\u003e\n            \u003cth scope=\"col\" class=\"px-3 py-3.5 text-left text-sm font-medium text-base-500\"\u003eTitle\u003c/th\u003e\n            \u003cth scope=\"col\" class=\"px-3 py-3.5 text-left text-sm font-medium text-base-500\"\u003eStatus\u003c/th\u003e\n          \u003c/tr\u003e\n        \u003c/thead\u003e\n        \u003ctbody class=\"divide-y divide-base-50 bg-white\"\u003e\n          \u003c!-- Table rows will go here --\u003e\n        \u003c/tbody\u003e\n      \u003c/table\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  \u003c/div\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis structure includes:\n\n* **&#96;flow-root&#96;**: Creates an independent positioning context.\n* **&#96;overflow-x-auto&#96;**: Adds horizontal scrolling for smaller screens.\n* Responsive padding classes like &#96;sm:px-6&#96; and &#96;lg:px-8&#96; to adjust spacing for different screen sizes.\n* Semantic elements like &#96;\u003cthead\u003e&#96; and &#96;\u003ctbody\u003e&#96; to ensure accessibility.\n\nTailwind CSS provides two key table-specific utilities:\n\n* **&#96;table-auto&#96;**: Adjusts column widths dynamically based on content.\n* **&#96;table-fixed&#96;**: Enforces strict column width control.\n\nThis setup lays the groundwork for a responsive table. You can further enhance it with CSS Grid and Tailwind’s utility classes to make your tables even more adaptable.\n\n## Using CSS Grid for Responsive Tables\n\nCSS Grid, paired with Tailwind CSS, provides an effective way to create tables that look great and work well on any device. Together, these tools make it easy to design layouts that adjust beautifully to different screen sizes.\n\n### CSS Grid Basics for Tables\n\nCSS Grid helps you build flexible layouts, whether you’re designing a traditional table structure or a card-style layout for smaller screens. Here’s how you can set it up:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n.responsive-table {\n  display: grid;\n  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));\n  gap: 1rem;\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe &#96;minmax()&#96; function ensures that columns adapt to available space while maintaining a minimum width.\n\nFor mobile devices, where space is tight, you can transform table rows into card-like blocks for better readability:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n@media (max-width: 640px) {\n  .table-row {\n    display: grid;\n    grid-template-columns: 1fr;\n    border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;\n    padding: 1rem;\n    margin-bottom: 1rem;\n  }\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis approach makes data easier to digest on small screens.\n\n### Tailwind CSS Grid Utilities\n\nTailwind CSS speeds up the process with its utility-first approach. Here’s an example of how you can use it:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3 lg:grid-cols-4 gap-4\"\u003e\n  \u003cdiv class=\"p-4 bg-white shadow rounded\"\u003e\n    \u003cdiv class=\"font-bold\"\u003eProduct Name\u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003cdiv class=\"text-gray-600\"\u003eDescription\u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003cdiv class=\"text-right\"\u003ePrice\u003c/div\u003e\n  \u003c/div\u003e\n  \u003c!-- Add more items as needed --\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTailwind’s responsive classes, like &#96;md:grid-cols-3&#96; for medium screens and &#96;lg:grid-cols-4&#96; for larger screens, make it simple to adjust layouts for different devices.\n\n\u003e “CSS Grid is a powerful 2-dimensional layout system, handling both rows and columns, unlike flexbox, which is primarily 1-dimensional.”\n\nTailwind also offers utilities for spacing, such as &#96;gap-x-4&#96; for horizontal spacing and &#96;gap-y-2&#96; for vertical spacing. These help keep your table design clean and consistent:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"grid gap-x-4 gap-y-2 md:gap-6\"\u003e\n  \u003c!-- Table content --\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Designing for Mobile and Multiple Devices\n\n### Mobile-First Table Design\n\nCreating tables for mobile devices often requires a single-column layout. This approach stacks table data vertically, making it easier to read on smaller screens. By turning rows into card-like components, each piece of data gets its own space, avoiding the hassle of horizontal scrolling:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"grid grid-cols-1 gap-4 p-4\"\u003e\n  \u003cdiv class=\"bg-white rounded-lg shadow p-4\"\u003e\n    \u003cdiv class=\"font-bold text-gray-700\"\u003eProduct Name\u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003cdiv class=\"text-gray-600\"\u003eDescription\u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003cdiv class=\"mt-2 text-right\"\u003ePrice\u003c/div\u003e\n  \u003c/div\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nPair semantic HTML with Tailwind’s utility classes to ensure your design is both clean and accessible:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv role=\"table\" aria-label=\"Products\" class=\"grid grid-cols-1 gap-4\"\u003e\n  \u003cdiv role=\"row\" class=\"bg-white p-4 rounded shadow\"\u003e\n    \u003cdiv role=\"cell\" class=\"font-medium text-gray-900\"\u003eCell Content\u003c/div\u003e\n  \u003c/div\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Adding Breakpoints for Larger Screens\n\nTailwind’s breakpoint utilities make it easy to adapt your tables for larger screens. You can progressively add columns, starting with one on mobile and scaling up to four on desktops:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"grid \n  grid-cols-1 \n  sm:grid-cols-2 \n  md:grid-cols-3 \n  lg:grid-cols-4 \n  gap-4 p-4\"\n\u003e\n  \u003c!-- Table content --\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nFor more complex tables, consider using conditional rendering. This allows you to show detailed views on larger screens while keeping things simple on mobile:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"hidden md:block\"\u003e\n  \u003c!-- Detailed view for larger screens --\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"md:hidden\"\u003e\n  \u003c!-- Simplified view for mobile --\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTo maintain consistent spacing, use Tailwind’s gap utilities like &#96;gap-x-4&#96; and &#96;gap-y-2&#96;. These help ensure that your layout remains visually balanced as you add more columns:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"grid \n  grid-cols-1 \n  md:grid-cols-3 \n  gap-x-4 \n  gap-y-2 \n  md:gap-6\"\n\u003e\n  \u003c!-- Table content --\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWith these responsive techniques in place, you can focus on improving usability and fine-tuning performance to deliver a smooth experience across all devices.\n\n## Improving Usability and Performance\n\n### Making Tables More Accessible\n\nDid you know that over 71% of users with disabilities depend on assistive technologies? \\[1\\] Ensuring tables are accessible is a key step in creating responsive designs that work for everyone. Here are some practical ways to make your tables more inclusive:\n\n* **ARIA Labels**: Add &#96;aria-label&#96; attributes to describe the table’s purpose. For example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003ctable role=\"table\" aria-label=\"Product Inventory\"\u003e\n  \u003ctr role=\"row\"\u003e\n    \u003cth role=\"columnheader\" scope=\"col\"\u003eProduct\u003c/th\u003e\n  \u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n* **Keyboard Navigation**: Use proper &#96;tabindex&#96; values to ensure users can navigate logically through the table.\n* **Data Labels**: Use &#96;data-label&#96; attributes to keep context clear, especially on mobile:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003ctd role=\"cell\" data-label=\"Product\"\u003eItem Name\u003c/td\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThese adjustments are especially helpful for mobile users, where responsive layouts can sometimes make important details harder to follow. By addressing accessibility, you’re improving usability for everyone.\n\n### Boosting Table Performance\n\nLarge tables can slow down page load times, particularly on mobile devices. And here’s why that matters: Amazon found that even a 1-second delay in load time can cut conversions by 7%. To avoid this, follow these steps to improve table performance:\n\n* **Lazy Loading**: Use the Intersection Observer API to load table rows only when they’re visible. This reduces initial load time and conserves memory.\n* **Smart Styling**: Take advantage of utility classes like those in Tailwind CSS to manage styling efficiently:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"overflow-auto\"\u003e\n  \u003ctable class=\"min-w-full divide-y divide-gray-200\"\u003e\n    \u003ctbody class=\"divide-y divide-gray-200\"\u003e\n      \u003c!-- Dynamically loaded content --\u003e\n    \u003c/tbody\u003e\n  \u003c/table\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis approach not only ensures smooth scrolling but also optimizes memory use, which is critical for devices with limited resources \\[2\\]. By focusing on both usability and performance, your tables will be ready to meet the expectations of today’s web users.\n\n## Testing and Debugging Tables\n\nTesting tables on various devices ensures they work well and align with design goals. Here’s how to test and troubleshoot effectively.\n\n### Testing and Debugging Responsive Tables\n\nChrome DevTools is a handy tool for examining responsive tables. Its Layout panel lets you visualize grid structures by enabling grid overlays on elements using &#96;display: grid&#96;. For more thorough testing, platforms like Testsigma allow cross-device testing on over 2000 iOS and Android devices, making it easier to handle complex layouts.\n\nHere are some quick fixes for common mobile table issues:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003c!-- Horizontal Overflow --\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"overflow-auto\"\u003e\n  \u003ctable class=\"min-w-full\"\u003e\n    \u003c!-- Table content --\u003e\n  \u003c/table\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n\u003c!-- Grid Alignment --\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-3 gap-4\"\u003e\n  \u003c!-- Table content --\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhen testing responsive tables, keep these tips in mind:\n\n* Use real content instead of placeholder text.\n* Confirm that keyboard navigation is smooth and functional.\n* Test table behavior at different screen widths.\n* Check compatibility across multiple browsers.\n\nAdditionally, tools like NVDA or VoiceOver can help ensure table content remains accessible and clear when adjusted for mobile layouts. These strategies will help you create tables that work well on any device.\n\n## Conclusion: Key Points and Next Steps\n\n### Best Practices Summary\n\nBuilding responsive tables starts with a **mobile-first approach**, using CSS Grid and Tailwind utilities to create layouts that adapt well to different devices. This method ensures your tables stay easy to use and accessible, without sacrificing performance or usability.\n\nWith these basics in place, it’s time to look at tools that can make your responsive table designs even better.\n\n### Additional Resources and Learning\n\nUsing the right tools can simplify your workflow and solve common issues with responsive tables. For instance, **Chrome DevTools** helps you visualize grids and debug layouts, while the **Tailwind CSS documentation** offers practical guidance for responsive design. To test your designs across multiple devices, **Hoverify** can save time and effort.\n\nHere’s a quick overview of these tools:\n\n| Tool              | Purpose                              |\n| ----------------- | ------------------------------------ |\n| Chrome DevTools   | Visualize grids and debug layouts    |\n| Tailwind CSS Docs | Explore responsive design techniques |\n| Hoverify          | Preview designs on multiple devices  |\n\nThese tools are especially helpful for solving problems like grid alignment, breakpoint testing, and ensuring accessibility on different screens.\n\nKeep in mind, creating responsive tables is an ongoing process. Regular testing, gathering user feedback, and tweaking based on performance data will help you deliver tables that look great and work well on any device.\n\n## FAQs\n\n### How to make a table responsive using Tailwind?\n\nCreating responsive tables in Tailwind CSS involves using utility classes to adapt the table layout for different screen sizes. Here’s an example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cdiv class=\"overflow-x-auto\"\u003e\n  \u003ctable class=\"min-w-full border-collapse block md:table\"\u003e\n    \u003cthead class=\"block md:table-header-group\"\u003e\n      \u003ctr class=\"border border-gray-200 md:border-none block md:table-row\"\u003e\n        \u003cth class=\"p-2 text-left font-medium md:border md:border-gray-200 block md:table-cell\"\u003eName\u003c/th\u003e\n        \u003cth class=\"p-2 text-left font-medium md:border md:border-gray-200 block md:table-cell\"\u003eEmail\u003c/th\u003e\n        \u003cth class=\"p-2 text-left font-medium md:border md:border-gray-200 block md:table-cell\"\u003eRole\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003c/thead\u003e\n    \u003ctbody class=\"block md:table-row-group\"\u003e\n      \u003c!-- Table content --\u003e\n    \u003c/tbody\u003e\n  \u003c/table\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTo ensure the table works well across devices, follow these steps:\n\n* Use utilities like &#96;block md:table&#96; to toggle between stacked and table layouts based on screen size.\n* Add &#96;border-separate&#96; and &#96;border-spacing-y-2&#96; for consistent row spacing.\n\n\u003e “We need to add some spacing between each of the rows which we can do using Tailwind’s Border spacing for tables. Let’s also add the default text size of small and wrap the table in a div so we can center it using flex.” - Daniel Salvado, a software developer and author at Evodeck Software, highlights the importance of spacing and alignment in responsive table design \\[2\\].\n\nAdditionally, use &#96;whitespace-nowrap&#96; to avoid text wrapping in cells, ensuring the table remains clean and easy to read on smaller screens. In this tutorial, Aleks will show you how to create your own cinematic video button in Framer.\n\n  \n## Step 1: Draw a Frame and Insert a Video\n\nBegin by drawing a frame, which will serve as the background of your button. You can resize the frame and round the corners to your liking. Once you have your frame, insert a video and scale it up to the width of your button. Drag the video into your frame and upload it.\n\n## Step 2: Add Text and Style Your Button\n\nNext, add text and an icon to your button. Style it however you want. With both the text and icon selected, hit ⌥ +⌘+ ⏎ to add a stack. Then drag the stack into the frame. To make your text more readable, lower the video's opacity a little bit.\n\n## Step 3: Create a Component\n\nSelect your button and create a component. Add a variant, and up the video opacity back to 1\\. Add a pointer cursor to the primary variant. Finally, link up the variants using \"mouse enter/leave.\"\n\n## Step 4: Add a Hover Effect (Optional)\n\nYou can stop here, but if you want to add an extra touch of flair, you can add a hover effect. Select your button component and add an overlay. Style it however you want, then drag in another video block.       "chunk": "Logo\n\nCase Studies\n\nServices\n\nFree Tools\n\nAbout\n\nWhat We Build\n\n Contact UsContact Us\n\nLogo\n\nLogo\n\nCase Studies\n\nServices\n\nFree Tools\n\nAbout\n\n Contact UsContact Us\n\nTable of Contents\n\n1\\. Motion Component Usage\n\n2\\. AnimatePresence for Dynamic Lists\n\n3\\. Layout Animations\n\n4\\. Gesture Animations\n\n5\\. Advanced Transitions\n\n6\\. Utilising Hooks in Framer Motion\n\nConclusion\n\nGet tips \u0026 tricks on building with no code and AI\n\nGet tips \u0026 tricks on building with no code and AI\n\nWe send a weekly newsletter letter helping share our insights on low code and AI to give you a competitive advantage.\n\n19 Mar 2025\n\n# Framer Motion Examples: Create Stunning Web Animations\n\nHarish Malhi - founder of Goodspeed\n\nHarish Malhi - founder of Goodspeed\n\nHarish Malhi\n\nGraphic showcasing Framer motion with Goodspeed logo \n\nGraphic showcasing Framer motion with Goodspeed logo \n\nGraphic showcasing Framer motion with Goodspeed logo \n\n**Animations play a vital role in** **enhancing user experience** by making web interactions more engaging and intuitive. However, implementing animations from scratch using CSS or JavaScript can be tedious, requiring significant effort to ensure smooth transitions and optimal performance. This is where Framer Motion simplifies the process.\n\nFramer Motion is a powerful React-based animation library that allows developers to create **fluid, high-performance animations** with minimal effort. Whether you want to add subtle UI enhancements or complex motion sequences, Framer Motion provides an intuitive approach to integrating animations into web projects. \n\nIn this guide, we will explore practical Framer Motion examples, covering essential features like motion components, AnimatePresence, and layout animations—all with real-world applications to improve interactive web design.\n\n## 1\\. Motion Component Usage\n\nMotion components form the foundation of Framer Motion, allowing you to transform standard HTML elements into animated components effortlessly. Unlike traditional CSS animations, Framer Motion offers a more dynamic approach with fine-grained control over transitions, easing functions, and interactive triggers.\n\n### 1.1 Understanding Motion Components\n\nFramer Motion’s **motion** API extends basic elements like div, span, and button, enabling them to animate seamlessly. This removes the complexity of handling keyframes manually and ensures **hardware-accelerated animations** for better performance.\n\nFor example, instead of defining CSS transitions, you can animate an element with just a few lines of code:\n\n\u003cmotion.div animate={{ opacity: 1, scale: 1.2 }} initial={{ opacity: 0, scale: 0.8 }} transition={{ duration: 0.5 }} /\u003e\n\nThis flexibility makes it easier to build engaging web animations that respond to user interactions. Additionally, optimised animations help retain visitors, considering that 53% of mobile users abandon a website that takes longer than three seconds to load. Ensuring animations are **lightweight and efficient is crucial for performance.**\n\n### 1.2 Example: Animated Emoji Cards\n\nA practical application of motion components is creating animated emoji cards. This Framer Motion example brings playful motion to UI elements, making them more visually engaging.\n\n\u003cmotion.div className=\"card\"   \nvariants={cardVariants}\u003e{emoji}\u003c/motion.div\u003e\n\nSuch dynamic interactions are valuable for e-commerce websites and marketing landing pages, where motion effects can guide users toward key actions.\n\nIf you’re working on a Framer website, consider pairing Framer Motion with our high-performance Framer templates to enhance branding. Learn more in our Guide to Choosing the Right Framer Template for Your Startup.\n\n## 2\\. AnimatePresence for Dynamic Lists\n\nManaging animations for elements that enter or exit the DOM is often a challenge. AnimatePresence, a core feature of Framer Motion, ensures that disappearing elements animate smoothly instead of being removed abruptly. This is particularly useful for **modals, notifications, and dynamic lists**.\n\n### 2.1 Exploring AnimatePresence\n\nBy default, React removes unmounted components immediately, leading to choppy transitions. AnimatePresence solves this by detecting component removal and allowing animations to complete before deletion.\n\nFor instance, when implementing tabbed navigation, removing a tab instantly can feel jarring. With AnimatePresence, you can apply smooth fade-out effects to inactive tabs, improving the flow of transitions.\n\n\u003cAnimatePresence\u003e\n\n {isVisible \u0026\u0026 (\n\n \u003cmotion.div exit={{ opacity: 0, scale: 0.9 }} transition={{ duration: 0.3 }}\u003e\n\n Content here\n\n \u003c/motion.div\u003e\n\n )}\n\n\u003c/AnimatePresence\u003e\n\nThis subtle improvement enhances user experience, making interactions **feel more intuitive and polished**.\n\n### 2.2 Example: Dynamic Tabs Animation\n\nImagine an interactive dashboard where users switch between analytics reports. Instead of a sudden shift, animated tab transitions make navigation more seamless. Below is an example of tab animations using AnimatePresence:\n\n\u003cAnimatePresence mode=\"wait\"\u003e\n\n \u003cmotion.div key={selectedTab.label} animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }} exit={{ opacity: 0, y: -20 }} transition={{ duration: 0.15 }}\u003e\n\n {selectedTab.icon}\n\n \u003c/motion.div\u003e\n\n\u003c/AnimatePresence\u003e\n\nThis technique is widely used in progressive web apps (PWAs) to enhance mobile responsiveness.\n\n## 3\\. Layout Animations\n\nModern web applications rely on fluid layout shifts to improve responsiveness. Whether you’re designing a **toggle switch, expanding a menu, or a reordering list**, Framer Motion’s layout property allows components to animate their position changes smoothly.\n\n### 3.1 The Layout Property\n\nTraditional layout changes can feel abrupt, leading to a disjointed experience. Framer Motion’s **layout** prop automatically detects element size adjustments and animates them with a natural flow. This is especially beneficial for:\n\n* **Interactive dashboards** where charts resize dynamically\n* **Navigation menus** that expand or collapse smoothly\n* **Form fields** that adjust based on user input\n\n\u003cmotion.div layout transition={{ type: \"spring\", stiffness: 500, damping: 30 }} /\u003e\n\nThis small addition creates a more polished user experience, keeping transitions sleek and lag-free.\n\n### 3.2 Example: Toggle Switch Animation\n\nLet’s take a common UI element—a toggle switch. Using Framer Motion’s layout prop, we can create an intuitive animation that smoothly shifts when toggled.\n\n\u003cdiv className=\"switch\" data-isOn={isOn} onClick={toggleSwitch}\u003e\n\n \u003cmotion.div className=\"handle\" layout transition={spring} /\u003e\n\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\nSuch micro-interactions improve user engagement, as they provide immediate feedback to actions.\n\nIf you’re optimising a Framer template for speed, you’ll also want to ensure animations don’t slow your site. Read Optimising Your Framer Template for Speed and Performance: Tips and Tricks.\n\n## 4\\. Gesture Animations\n\nGesture animations create responsive and engaging user experiences by reacting to user actions like **hovering, clicking, or dragging**. These micro-interactions make web interfaces feel more intuitive and dynamic.\n\n### 4.1 Handling Gestures in Framer Motion\n\nFramer Motion provides **gesture-based animations** using properties like:\n\n* whileHover – Triggers effects when a user hovers over an element.\n* whileTap – Responds when an element is clicked or tapped.\n* drag – Enables elements to be moved interactively.\n\nFor instance, an interactive button can change its appearance based on user interaction, improving usability:\n\n\u003cmotion.button whileHover={{ scale: 1.1 }} whileTap={{ scale: 0.9 }}\u003e\n\n Click Me\n\n\u003c/motion.button\u003e\n\n### 4.2 Example: Interactive Button\n\nA great use case for gesture animations is interactive buttons that respond to hover and tap interactions. Below is an example of a star rating button that reacts when hovered or clicked:\n\n\u003cmotion.button\n\n initial={false}\n\n animate={\\[isLiked ? \"liked\" : \"unliked\", isHover ? \"hover\" : \"rest\"\\]}\n\n whileTap=\"press\"\n\n variants={buttonVariants}\n\n onHoverStart={() =\u003e setIsHover(true)}\n\n onHoverEnd={() =\u003e setIsHover(false)}\n\n onClick={() =\u003e setIsLiked(!isLiked)}\n\n\\\u003e\n\n \u003cmotion.div className=\"icon\" variants={{ liked: { opacity: 0 } }}\u003e\n\n \u003cStarIcon isHover={isHover} isLiked={isLiked} /\u003e\n\n \u003c/motion.div\u003e\n\n\u003c/motion.button\u003e\n\nThis type of **real-time feedback** **improves user interaction**, making buttons more engaging and functional.\n\nIf you're customising Framer templates and want to improve UI interactivity, check out Customising Your Framer Template: A Guide for Beginners.\n\n## 5\\. Advanced Transitions\n\nBasic animations work well for simple effects, but for more dynamic interactions, Framer Motion allows fine-tuned transition control, such as **spring physics, staggered animations, and animated numbers**.\n\n### 5.1 Creating Complex Transitions\n\nFramer Motion’s transitions go beyond simple fade effects. It allows for **spring-based movements**, **delayed animations**, and **custom bezier curves** for smoother effects.\n\nKey transition properties include:\n\n* spring – Creates **realistic, physics-based motion**.\n* easeInOut – Smoothens animations for a **natural flow**.\n* staggerChildren – Adds a **cascading delay** to multiple elements.\n\nFor example, a sequential loading animation can be achieved with:\n\n\u003cmotion.div variants={{ hidden: { opacity: 0 }, visible: { opacity: 1, transition: { staggerChildren: 0.2 } } }}\u003e\n\n \u003cmotion.div variants={{ hidden: { y: 10 }, visible: { y: 0 } }} /\u003e\n\n \u003cmotion.div variants={{ hidden: { y: 10 }, visible: { y: 0 } }} /\u003e\n\n\u003c/motion.div\u003e\n\n### 5.2 Example: Animating Numerical Values\n\nA common use case is animating counters or statistics, often seen in dashboards or progress indicators. If you're designing dashboards or analytic pages, don't miss our walkthrough on how to conduct a Framer performance audit.\n\nconst count = useMotionValue(0);\n\nconst rounded = useTransform(count, Math.round);\n\nuseEffect(() =\u003e {\n\n animate(count, 100, { duration: 10 });\n\n}, \\[\\]);\n\nreturn \u003cmotion.h1\u003e{rounded}\u003c/motion.h1\u003e;\n\nBy dynamically updating numeric values, this example creates a smooth counter animation, perfect for analytics dashboards or pricing displays.\n\n## 6\\. Utilising Hooks in Framer Motion\n\nHooks provide additional flexibility in Framer Motion, enabling **parallax effects, scroll-based animations, and dynamic transformations**. These are crucial for smooth, modern web interactions.\n\n### 6.1 Introduction to Framer Motion Hooks\n\nHooks allow developers to capture real-time motion values and dynamically adjust animations. Some essential Framer Motion hooks include:\n\n* useScroll – Triggers animations **based on scroll position**.\n* useSpring – Smoothens animations **using spring physics**.\n* useTransform – Maps **one value to another**, enabling **responsive animations**.\n* useVelocity – Adjusts animation **speed dynamically**.\n\n### 6.2 Examples of Useful Hooks\n\n#### 6.2.1 useScroll for Parallax Effects\n\nParallax scrolling creates a **depth effect**, making backgrounds move slower than foreground elements:\n\nconst { scrollYProgress } = useScroll();\n\nconst yTransform = useTransform(scrollYProgress, \\[0, 1\\], \\[0, -200\\]);\n\nreturn \u003cmotion.div style={{ y: yTransform }}\u003eParallax Content\u003c/motion.div\u003e;\n\n#### 6.2.2 useSpring for Smooth Animations\n\nSprings create **natural motion curves** without requiring manual timing adjustments.\n\nconst x = useMotionValue(0);\n\nconst springX = useSpring(x, { stiffness: 300, damping: 30 });\n\nreturn \u003cmotion.div style={{ x: springX }} /\u003e;\n\n#### 6.2.3 useTransform for Responsive Animations\n\nTransforms allow **adaptive motion** based on dynamic input values.\n\nconst scale = useTransform(scrollYProgress, \\[0, 1\\], \\[1, 1.5\\]);\n\nreturn \u003cmotion.div style={{ scale }}\u003eScaling Effect\u003c/motion.div\u003e;\n\n#### 6.2.4 useVelocity for Dynamic Speed Adjustments\n\nBy tracking **scroll speed**, useVelocity creates **adaptive motion effects**.\n\nconst scrollSpeed = useVelocity(scrollY);\n\nconst moveX = useTransform(scrollSpeed, \\[-1000, 1000\\], \\[-50, 50\\]);\n\nreturn \u003cmotion.div style={{ x: moveX }}\u003eMoving Element\u003c/motion.div\u003e;\n\nFramer Motion is a game-changer for web developers and designers looking to enhance UI with animations. Unlike traditional CSS animations, its **motion components, AnimatePresence, and layout animations** simplify the process while offering greater control. Whether you're creating **gesture-based interactions, complex transitions, or scroll-driven effects**, Framer Motion provides an intuitive way to build engaging and high-performance animations.\n\nBy leveraging motion hooks like **useScroll** and **useSpring**, you can create dynamic and responsive animations that not only improve aesthetics but also contribute to better user retention. Considering that 75% of users judge a company's credibility based on website design, investing in seamless animations is no longer optional—it's a necessity.\n\nNeed more help planning your website animations? Get the expert Framer guidance you need- just book a free consultation. \n\nGet tips \u0026 tricks building with no code and AI\n\nEvery week, you'll get first hand insights of building with no code and AI so you get a competitive advantage\n\n##### More from our blog\n\n##### More from our blog\n\n View all blogsView all blogs View all blogsView all blogs\n\nHomepage screenshot of Justica, Framer template designed for legal professionalsHomepage screenshot of Justica, Framer template designed for legal professionalsFramerTag26 Sept 2024Justica: Elevating Your Law Firm's Online PresenceHarish Malhi - Report Abuse \n\nCover image for A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation \n\nAustin Welsh \n\nAustin Welsh \n\n Posted on Feb 17 \n\n#  A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation\n\n#webdev #ui #react #javascript \n\n👋 **Let's Connect!** Follow me on GitHub for new projects.\n\n---\n\n## **Introduction** \n\nBuilding **consistent and scalable UI components** is crucial in modern web development. **Storybook** is a tool that allows developers to **isolate, develop, test, and document UI components** in a sandboxed environment. \n\nStorybook enables you to:  \n  \n✅ **Develop components in isolation** without running a full application.  \n  \n✅ **Create a component library** for design consistency.  \n  \n✅ **Test and document UI behavior** interactively.  \n  \n✅ **Integrate with frameworks like React, Vue, Angular, and more**. \n\nIn this comprehensive guide, we’ll cover: \n\n* **Setting up Storybook**\n* **Writing and organizing stories**\n* **Using add-ons and controls**\n* **Testing components with Storybook**\n* **Mocking API requests**\n* **Visual regression testing**\n* **Automating accessibility testing**\n* **Snapshot testing**\n* **Theming in Storybook**\n* **Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E testing**\n* **Deploying Storybook as documentation**\n* **Best practices for Storybook projects**\n\n---\n\n##  What is Storybook?\n\nStorybook is an open-source tool for **building UI components in isolation**. It provides a dedicated environment for testing and documenting components **without running the entire application**. \n\n### **Why Use Storybook?** \n\n| Feature                                                | Storybook |\n| ------------------------------------------------------ | --------- |\n| Develop components **in isolation**                    | ✅ Yes     |\n| Interactive **component preview**                      | ✅ Yes     |\n| Built-in **documentation generation**                  | ✅ Yes     |\n| Supports **multiple frameworks** (React, Vue, Angular) | ✅ Yes     |\n| Integration with **Jest, Testing Library, Playwright** | ✅ Yes     |\n\n---\n\n##  Installing and Setting Up Storybook\n\nStorybook can be installed in a new or existing project. \n\n### **Installation for React** \n\nRun the following command in your project directory:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook@latest init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Automatically detects the framework and **configures Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ Generates a &#96;.storybook&#96; folder with configuration files.  \n  \n✔ Creates example stories to get started. \n\n### **Starting Storybook** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStorybook will launch on &#96;http://localhost:6006/&#96;.\n\n---\n\n##  Writing Your First Story\n\nA **story** represents a UI component's **state**. It defines how the component should appear in different scenarios. \n\n### **Basic Button Story (React Example)** \n\nCreate a file **&#96;Button.stories.js&#96;** inside &#96;src/components/Button/&#96;.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from 'react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\nexport default {\n  title: 'Components/Button',\n  component: Button,\n};\n\nexport const Primary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Primary Button\" /\u003e;\nexport const Secondary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Secondary Button\" variant=\"secondary\" /\u003e;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each **export** represents a different **state of the component**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;title&#96; defines the **category in Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;component&#96; links the **UI component** to the story. \n\n---\n\n##  Using Controls for Dynamic Interaction\n\nStorybook Controls allow developers to modify props dynamically in the UI.\n\n###  Example: Adding Controls to Button\n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nexport const Playground = (args) =\u003e \u003cButton {...args} /\u003e;\n\nPlayground.args = {\n  label: 'Dynamic Button',\n  variant: 'primary',\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nNow, Storybook will provide a UI panel where developers can change **label** and **variant** dynamically.\n\n✔ Helps **test different states** without modifying the code.\n\n---\n\n##  Enhancing Storybook with Add-ons\n\nStorybook Add-ons extend functionality.\n\n###  Popular Storybook Add-ons\n\n| Add-on                     | Purpose                  |\n| -------------------------- | ------------------------ |\n| @storybook/addon-controls  | Adjust props dynamically |\n| @storybook/addon-docs      | Generate documentation   |\n| @storybook/addon-a11y      | Accessibility testing    |\n| @storybook/testing-library | UI interaction testing   |\n\n###  Installing an Add-on\n\nExample: Installing the **Accessibility Add-on**  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @storybook/addon-a11y --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; to **register the add-on**:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Adds an \"Accessibility\" panel to test contrast, ARIA attributes, and color issues.\n\n---\n\n##  Organizing Stories for Scalability\n\nA well-structured Storybook project improves maintainability. \n\n### **Recommended Folder Structure** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n📂 src\n ┣ 📂 components\n ┃ ┣ 📂 Button\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.stories.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.test.js\n ┣ 📂 .storybook\n ┃ ┣ 📜 main.js   # Configurations\n ┃ ┣ 📜 preview.js  # Global decorators\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each component has **its own folder** for easy organization.  \n  \n✔ &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; manages **configurations** and **add-ons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Automating Accessibility Testing in Storybook\n\nEnsuring your UI components are **accessible** is crucial for usability. Storybook integrates with **accessibility testing tools** to automatically detect potential issues.\n\n### **Installing the Accessibility Add-on** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-a11y\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Enabling the Add-on** \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Accessibility Tests** \n\nWhen the Storybook UI loads, a new **\"Accessibility\" panel** appears, displaying any detected issues.\n\n✔ Automatically **checks for contrast issues, missing ARIA attributes, and keyboard accessibility**.  \n  \n✔ Helps fix **WCAG compliance issues** before production. \n\n---\n\n##  Visual Regression Testing in Storybook\n\n**Visual Regression Testing** detects UI changes by comparing rendered components **before and after updates**. This ensures that UI modifications do not introduce **unintended design changes**.\n\n### **Installing Visual Testing Add-ons** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-visual-tests\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Adding a Screenshot Test** \n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { within, userEvent } from '@storybook/testing-library';\n\nexport const VisualTest = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Click me\" /\u003e;\n\nVisualTest.play = async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n  const canvas = within(canvasElement);\n  const button = canvas.getByRole('button');\n  await userEvent.click(button);\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Visual Tests** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Detects UI changes with **automatic snapshot comparisons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Mocking API Calls in Storybook\n\nStorybook can mock API requests to test UI behavior without relying on a backend.\n\n###  Example: Mocking an API Response\n\nInstall Mock Service Worker (MSW):  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install msw --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;mocks.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { setupWorker, rest } from 'msw';\n\nexport const worker = setupWorker(\n  rest.get('/api/user', (req, res, ctx) =\u003e {\n    return res(ctx.json({ name: 'Mock User' }));\n  })\n);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStart the mock server in &#96;preview.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { worker } from '../mocks';\n\nworker.start();\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Components now receive mock API responses during development.\n\n---\n\n##  Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E Testing\n\nStorybook can be used with **Playwright** to perform **end-to-end (E2E) testing** for UI components.\n\n### **Installing Playwright** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @playwright/test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Writing a Playwright Test for a Storybook Component** \n\nCreate a file &#96;Button.spec.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst { test, expect } = require('@playwright/test');\n\ntest('Check if Button component renders', async ({ page }) =\u003e {\n    await page.goto('http://localhost:6006/?path=/story/components-button--primary');\n    const button = await page.locator('button');\n    await expect(button).toHaveText('Primary Button');\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running the Playwright Test** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx playwright test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ **Combines UI component testing with full browser automation**. \n\n---\n\n##  Writing Component Tests in Storybook\n\nStorybook integrates with Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright for UI testing.\n\n###  Example: Testing with Jest + Testing Library\n\nInstall dependencies:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @testing-library/react jest --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;Button.test.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\ntest('renders the button', () =\u003e {\n  render(\u003cButton label=\"Click Me\" /\u003e);\n  expect(screen.getByText('Click Me')).toBeInTheDocument();\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Ensures components render correctly.  \n✔ Runs with npm test.\n\n---\n\n##  Deploying Storybook as Documentation\n\nStorybook can be deployed as a **component documentation site**.\n\n### **Generate Static Build** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run build-storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis creates a **&#96;storybook-static/&#96;** folder.\n\n### **Deploy to GitHub Pages** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Makes Storybook accessible via **GitHub Pages or any static host**. \n\n---\n\n##  Running Storybook in CI/CD\n\nIntegrating Storybook in CI/CD pipelines ensures UI consistency across development.\n\n###  GitHub Actions Example\n\nCreate &#96;.github/workflows/storybook.yml&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nname: Storybook CI\non: push\njobs:\n  test:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - name: Checkout Code\n        uses: actions/checkout@v2\n      - name: Install Dependencies\n        run: npm install\n      - name: Build Storybook\n        run: npm run build-storybook\n      - name: Deploy Storybook\n        run: npx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Runs Storybook on every code push.\n\n---\n\n##  Best Practices for Storybook Projects\n\n✔ **Use Controls \u0026 Docs Add-ons** for **dynamic component interaction**.  \n  \n✔ **Organize components by category** (&#96;Components/Button&#96; vs &#96;Components/Inputs&#96;).  \n  \n✔ **Automate visual \u0026 snapshot testing** to **catch unintended changes**.  \n  \n✔ **Deploy Storybook** as **live documentation** for developers \u0026 designers.  \n  \n✔ **Integrate Storybook in CI/CD** to ensure UI consistency. \n\n---\n\n## **Conclusion** \n\nStorybook is a **powerful tool for UI development, testing, and documentation**. It improves **component reusability, consistency, and collaboration** across teams. \n\n🚀 **Next Steps:**  \n  \n✅ Install Storybook and create your first component story.  \n  \n✅ Experiment with **Controls \u0026 Add-ons**.  \n  \n✅ Integrate Storybook into your **CI/CD pipeline**. \n\n---\n\n### **Tags** \n\nStorybook #Frontend #Testing #UIDevelopment #ComponentLibrary \n\n---\n\n###  TLDR – Highlights for Skimmers\n\n* Storybook isolates UI components for development and testing.\n* Controls allow dynamic prop changes inside Storybook UI.\n* Add-ons extend functionality (accessibility, documentation, testing).\n* Supports Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright for UI testing.\n* Mocks API responses with MSW for frontend testing.\n* Can be deployed as documentation on GitHub Pages or other platforms.\n\n---\n\n💬 **Have you used Storybook?** Share your experience in the comments!\n\n##  Top comments (1) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCollapse Expand \n\naustinwdigital profile image \n\nAustin Welsh \n\n Austin Welsh \n\n Austin Welsh \n\nFollow \n\n Senior Full Stack Developer @ Disney | JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Next.js\n\n* Location  \n United States\n* Work  \n Senior Full Stack Developer @ Disney\n* Joined  \nDec 21, 2024\n\n•  Feb 17 \n\nDropdown menu \n\n* Copy link\n* Hide\n\nWhat do you mainly use Storybook for?\n\nA) Component Development  \nB) UI Testing  \nC) Documentation  \nD) Something else\n\nLet me know!\n\nLike comment: Like comment: 1 like  Like Comment button Reply \n\n Some comments may only be visible to logged-in visitors.
