      "chunk": "DronaHQ Logo  \n\n# Engineer's Guide: Building a React Component Library From Scratch\n\n Need custom internal tools, minus the usual dev marathon?  Try DronaHQ Free  —Go from zero to deployed app in an afternoon!\n\n### TL;DR: Engineer's Quick Start\n\nThis guide walks engineers through building a React component library from scratch. Key steps include:\n\n* **Setup a robust project:** Initialize with React, TypeScript, Rollup (for bundling), Jest/RTL (for testing), and Storybook (for development/documentation).\n* **Structure for scalability:** Organize components, hooks, styles, and utilities for easy maintenance and growth.\n* **Build \u0026 Test Components:** Develop individual UI components (e.g., a Button example provided), write comprehensive unit tests, and create interactive Storybook stories for documentation.\n* **Publish \u0026 Version:** Configure your &#96;package.json&#96; correctly and use npm (or a private registry) to publish your versioned library effectively.\n* **Consider Advanced Topics:** Implement accessibility (A11y), theming strategies, performance optimizations, and helpful utility hooks to create a production-ready, professional-grade library.\n\n**Table of Contents** \n* 1\\. Introduction: Why Build a Component Library?\n* 2\\. Core Project Setup \u0026 Essential Tooling\n* 3\\. Structuring Your Library for Maintainability\n* 4\\. Crafting Your First Component (Button Example)\n* 5\\. Comprehensive Testing \u0026 Storybook Integration\n* 6\\. Publishing \u0026 Versioning Your Library\n* 7\\. Advanced Considerations for Robust Libraries\n* 8\\. Conclusion \u0026 Best Practices\n\n## 1\\. Introduction: Why Build a Component Library?\n\nAs an engineer, you understand the value of DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles and maintainable code. A **React component library** embodies these by providing a centralized, versioned collection of reusable UI elements. For internal tools, this means:\n\n* **Consistency:** Ensuring all internal applications share a cohesive look, feel, and behavior.\n* **Efficiency:** Accelerating development by providing pre-built, tested UI building blocks.\n* **Maintainability:** Simplifying updates and bug fixes—change a component in the library, and it updates across all consuming applications (with version control).\n* **Quality:** Enforcing best practices, accessibility standards, and thorough testing at the component level.\n\nThis guide focuses on the technical execution of building such a library. For a higher-level overview on planning and strategy, refer to resources aimed at engineering management.\n\n## 2\\. Core Project Setup \u0026 Essential Tooling\n\nSetting up your project correctly is crucial. We'll use TypeScript for type safety, Rollup for efficient bundling, Jest for testing, and Storybook for component development and documentation.\n\nStart by initializing a new npm package and installing essential development dependencies:\n\nCopy&#96;mkdir my-react-ui-library \u0026\u0026 cd my-react-ui-library\nnpm init -y\n# Core React and build tools\nnpm install --save-dev react react-dom typescript rollup @rollup/plugin-node-resolve @rollup/plugin-commonjs @rollup/plugin-typescript @babel/preset-react @babel/preset-typescript tslib\n# Testing tools\nnpm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom jest-environment-jsdom babel-jest\n# Storybook\nnpm install --save-dev storybook @storybook/react-webpack5 @storybook/addon-essentials @storybook/addon-interactions @storybook/testing-library webpack\n# Optional: for CSS handling in Rollup\nnpm install --save-dev rollup-plugin-postcss postcss&#96;\n\n**Configure &#96;tsconfig.json&#96;** for TypeScript compilation:\n\nCopy&#96;{\n  \"compilerOptions\": {\n    \"target\": \"ES6\",            // Target modern JavaScript\n    \"module\": \"ESNext\",         // Use ES modules for tree shaking\n    \"lib\": [\"dom\", \"dom.iterable\", \"esnext\"],\n    \"jsx\": \"react-jsx\",         // Use new JSX transform\n    \"declaration\": true,        // Generate .d.ts files\n    \"declarationDir\": \"dist/types\", // Output directory for .d.ts files\n    \"outDir\": \"dist\",           // Output directory for JS files (if not using Rollup for this)\n    \"rootDir\": \"src\",           // Source directory\n    \"strict\": true,             // Enable all strict type-checking options\n    \"esModuleInterop\": true,    // Enables emit interoperability between CommonJS and ES Modules\n    \"skipLibCheck\": true,       // Skip type checking of all declaration files (*.d.ts)\n    \"forceConsistentCasingInFileNames\": true,\n    \"moduleResolution\": \"node\",\n    \"resolveJsonModule\": true,\n    \"isolatedModules\": true,\n    \"noEmit\": true              // Let Rollup handle emits, TS only for type checking \u0026 declarations\n                                // Set to false if you want tsc to emit JS files alongside Rollup\n  },\n  \"include\": [\"src/**/*\"],      // Files to include for compilation\n  \"exclude\": [\"node_modules\", \"dist\", \"**/*.stories.tsx\", \"**/*.test.tsx\"]\n}&#96;\n\nNote: The &#96;\"noEmit\": true&#96; setting is common if Rollup is solely responsible for transpiling and bundling JS, while &#96;tsc&#96; is used for generating declaration files. Adjust if your setup differs.\n\n**Configure Babel (&#96;babel.config.js&#96;)** for Jest and Storybook (Rollup can use its own TypeScript plugin):\n\nCopy&#96;module.exports = {\n  presets: [\n    '@babel/preset-env', // For transpiling ES6+ down to ES5 if needed for older environments\n    '@babel/preset-react',\n    '@babel/preset-typescript',\n  ],\n};&#96;\n\n**Configure Rollup (&#96;rollup.config.js&#96;)** for bundling your library:\n\nCopy&#96;import resolve from '@rollup/plugin-node-resolve';\nimport commonjs from '@rollup/plugin-commonjs';\nimport typescript from '@rollup/plugin-typescript';\nimport postcss from 'rollup-plugin-postcss'; // If handling CSS\n// import { terser } from 'rollup-plugin-terser'; // For minification\n\nconst packageJson = require('./package.json');\n\nexport default {\n  input: 'src/index.ts', // Your library's entry point\n  output: [\n    {\n      file: packageJson.main,\n      format: 'cjs', // CommonJS for Node compatibility\n      sourcemap: true,\n    },\n    {\n      file: packageJson.module,\n      format: 'esm', // ES Module for tree shaking\n      sourcemap: true,\n    },\n  ],\n  plugins: [\n    resolve(),\n    commonjs(),\n    typescript({ tsconfig: './tsconfig.json', exclude: [\"**/*.test.tsx\", \"**/*.stories.tsx\"] }),\n    postcss({ // Example for handling CSS files\n      extract: 'styles.css', // Extracts CSS to a single file\n      minimize: true,\n    }),\n    // terser(), // Uncomment for production builds to minify\n  ],\n  external: ['react', 'react-dom'], // Externalize peer dependencies\n};&#96;\n\nEnsure your &#96;package.json&#96; has &#96;main&#96;, &#96;module&#96;, and &#96;types&#96; fields pointing to the Rollup outputs and declaration files respectively (see Publishing section).\n\n## 3\\. Structuring Your Library for Maintainability\n\nA clear folder structure is vital for a growing component library:\n\nCopy&#96;my-react-ui-library/\n├── dist/                     // Bundled output\n├── src/\n│   ├── index.ts              // Main export file for all public components/hooks\n│   ├── components/           // Directory for individual UI components\n│   │   └── Button/\n│   │       ├── Button.tsx    // Component logic and JSX\n│   │       ├── Button.module.css // Component-specific styles (CSS Modules example)\n│   │       ├── Button.stories.tsx // Storybook stories\n│   │       └── Button.test.tsx    // Jest/RTL tests\n│   │   └── AnotherComponent/\n│   ├── hooks/                // Reusable custom React hooks\n│   │   └── useSomeLogic.ts\n│   ├── styles/               // Global styles, design tokens, base styles\n│   │   ├── _variables.css    // CSS Variables for design tokens\n│   │   └── global.css\n│   └── utils/                // Shared utility functions\n│       └── helpers.ts\n├── .storybook/               // Storybook configuration\n├── jest.config.js            // Jest configuration\n├── rollup.config.js          // Rollup configuration\n├── tsconfig.json             // TypeScript configuration\n├── babel.config.js           // Babel configuration\n└── package.json&#96;\n\nYour main entry point &#96;src/index.ts&#96; should export everything you want to make public from your library:\n\nCopy&#96;// src/index.ts\nexport * from './components/Button/Button';\n// export * from './components/AnotherComponent/AnotherComponent';\n// export * from './hooks/useSomeLogic';\n// export * from './styles/global.css'; // If you want to allow global CSS import\n&#96;\n\n## 4\\. Crafting Your First Component (Button Example)\n\nLet's create a foundational &#96;Button&#96; component.\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.tsx&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;&#96; import React, { ButtonHTMLAttributes } from 'react';\nimport styles from './Button.module.css'; // Using CSS Modules\n\nexport interface ButtonProps extends ButtonHTMLAttributes\u003cHTMLButtonElement\u003e {\n  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'destructive';\n  size?: 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';\n  children: React.ReactNode; // Use children for the label or content\n}\n\nexport const Button: React.FC\u003cButtonProps\u003e = ({\n  children,\n  variant = 'primary',\n  size = 'medium',\n  className = '',\n  ...props\n}) =\u003e {\n  const modeClass = styles[variant] || styles.primary;\n  const sizeClass = styles[size] || styles.medium;\n\n  return (\n    \u003cbutton\n      type=\"button\" // Default to type=\"button\" for accessibility unless overridden\n      className={&#96;${styles.buttonBase} ${modeClass} ${sizeClass} ${className}&#96;}\n      {...props}\n    \u003e\n      {children}\n    \u003c/button\u003e\n  );\n};\n &#96;&#96;\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.module.css&#96;** (Example using CSS Modules):\n\nCopy&#96;/* src/components/Button/Button.module.css */\n.buttonBase {\n  border: none;\n  padding: 10px 20px;\n  cursor: pointer;\n  font-family: inherit;\n  border-radius: 4px;\n  transition: background-color 0.2s ease-in-out, box-shadow 0.2s ease-in-out;\n  display: inline-flex;\n  align-items: center;\n  justify-content: center;\n  text-decoration: none; /* For anchor-like buttons */\n  font-weight: 700; /* Bolder for Montserrat */\n}\n\n.buttonBase:focus-visible {\n  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring-color, blue); /* Define --focus-ring-color in global styles */\n  outline-offset: 2px;\n}\n\n/* Variants */\n.primary {\n  background-color: var(--button-primary-bg, #007bff);\n  color: var(--button-primary-text, white);\n}\n.primary:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-primary-hover-bg, #0056b3);\n}\n\n.secondary {\n  background-color: var(--button-secondary-bg, #6c757d);\n  color: var(--button-secondary-text, white);\n}\n.secondary:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-secondary-hover-bg, #545b62);\n}\n\n.destructive {\n  background-color: var(--button-destructive-bg, #dc3545);\n  color: var(--button-destructive-text, white);\n}\n.destructive:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-destructive-hover-bg, #c82333);\n}\n\n/* Sizes */\n.small {\n  padding: 6px 12px;\n  font-size: 0.875rem;\n}\n.medium {\n  padding: 10px 20px;\n  font-size: 1rem;\n}\n.large {\n  padding: 12px 24px;\n  font-size: 1.125rem;\n}\n&#96;\n\nEnsure you define CSS variables like &#96;--button-primary-bg&#96; in your global styles (e.g., &#96;src/styles/_variables.css&#96;) for theming capabilities.\n\n## 5\\. Comprehensive Testing \u0026 Storybook Integration\n\n**Testing with Jest \u0026 React Testing Library:**\n\n**&#96;jest.config.js&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;module.exports = {\n  testEnvironment: 'jsdom',\n  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['\u003crootDir\u003e/jest.setup.js'], // if you have a setup file\n  moduleNameMapper: {\n    '\\\\.(css|less|scss|sass)$': 'identity-obj-proxy', // Mocks CSS Modules\n  },\n  transform: {\n    '^.+\\\\.(ts|tsx|js|jsx)$': 'babel-jest',\n  },\n};\n&#96;\n\nCreate &#96;jest.setup.js&#96; (optional, for global test setup like importing &#96;@testing-library/jest-dom&#96;):\n\nCopy&#96;// jest.setup.js\nimport '@testing-library/jest-dom';\n&#96;\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.test.tsx&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;import React from 'react';\nimport { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\ndescribe('Button Component', () =\u003e {\n  test('renders with children', () =\u003e {\n    render(\u003cButton\u003eClick Me\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /Click Me/i })).toBeInTheDocument();\n  });\n\n  test('applies variant and size classes correctly', () =\u003e {\n    render(\u003cButton variant=\"secondary\" size=\"large\"\u003eSubmit\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    const button = screen.getByRole('button', { name: /Submit/i });\n    // Note: Testing CSS module class names can be tricky. \n    // It's often better to test visual appearance via visual regression tests.\n    // However, you can check if base classes are applied if needed.\n    expect(button).toHaveClass('buttonBase'); // from Button.module.css, actual name might be mangled\n    // For specific variant/size classes, snapshot testing or visual testing is more robust.\n  });\n\n  test('calls onClick handler when clicked', () =\u003e {\n    const handleClick = jest.fn();\n    render(\u003cButton onClick={handleClick}\u003eTest Click\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Test Click'));\n    expect(handleClick).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);\n  });\n\n  test('is disabled when disabled prop is true', () =\u003e {\n    render(\u003cButton disabled\u003eDisabled Button\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /Disabled Button/i })).toBeDisabled();\n  });\n});\n&#96;\n\n**Storybook for Development and Documentation:**\n\nInitialize Storybook in your project:\n\nCopy&#96;npx storybook@latest init&#96;\n\nFollow the prompts. It should detect your React setup.\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.stories.tsx&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;import React from 'react';\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Button, ButtonProps } from './Button'; // Import ButtonProps\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003cButtonProps\u003e = { // Use ButtonProps for Meta type\n  title: 'Components/Button',    // How it will appear in Storybook navigation\n  component: Button,\n  tags: ['autodocs'],            // Enables auto-generated documentation\n  argTypes: {                   // Define controls for props\n    variant: {\n      control: { type: 'select' },\n      options: ['primary', 'secondary', 'destructive'],\n      description: 'The visual style of the button',\n    },\n    size: {\n      control: { type: 'select' },\n      options: ['small', 'medium', 'large'],\n      description: 'The size of the button',\n    },\n    children: {\n      control: 'text',\n      description: 'Button label or content',\n    },\n    disabled: {\n      control: 'boolean',\n      description: 'Disables the button',\n    },\n    onClick: {\n      action: 'clicked', // Logs clicks in the Storybook actions tab\n      description: 'Optional click handler',\n    },\n  },\n  parameters: {\n    layout: 'centered', // Centers the component in the Canvas tab\n  },\n};\n\nexport default meta;\n\n// Define a \"template\" story that maps args to the component\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003cButtonProps\u003e; // Use ButtonProps for Story type\n\nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Primary Button',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Secondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'secondary',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Secondary Button',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Destructive: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'destructive',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Delete',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const LargePrimary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    size: 'large',\n    children: 'Large Primary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const SmallSecondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'secondary',\n    size: 'small',\n    children: 'Small Secondary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Disabled: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    children: 'Disabled Button',\n    disabled: true,\n  },\n};\n&#96;\n\nRun Storybook with &#96;npm run storybook&#96;.\n\n## 6\\. Publishing \u0026 Versioning Your Library\n\nOnce your components are ready, you'll publish your library to a package registry (like npm or a private registry).\n\n**Update &#96;package.json&#96;** with necessary fields:\n\nCopy&#96;{\n  \"name\": \"my-react-ui-library\",\n  \"version\": \"0.1.0\",\n  \"private\": false, // Set to false to publish\n  \"description\": \"A fantastic React UI component library.\",\n  \"author\": \"Your Name \u003cyouremail@example.com\u003e\",\n  \"license\": \"MIT\", // Or your chosen license\n  \"repository\": {\n    \"type\": \"git\",\n    \"url\": \"https://github.com/yourusername/my-react-ui-library.git\" // Replace\n  },\n  \"main\": \"dist/index.cjs.js\", // CommonJS entry point from Rollup\n  \"module\": \"dist/index.esm.js\", // ES Module entry point from Rollup\n  \"types\": \"dist/types/index.d.ts\", // TypeScript definitions entry point\n  \"files\": [ // Files to include in the published package\n    \"dist\"\n  ],\n  \"scripts\": {\n    \"build\": \"rollup -c\", // Your build command\n    \"test\": \"jest\",\n    \"storybook\": \"storybook dev -p 6006\",\n    \"build-storybook\": \"storybook build\",\n    \"lint\": \"eslint src --ext .ts,.tsx\",\n    \"clean\": \"rm -rf dist\" // Script to clean the dist folder\n  },\n  \"peerDependencies\": { // Specify peer dependencies\n    \"react\": \"^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0\",\n    \"react-dom\": \"^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0\"\n  },\n  \"devDependencies\": {\n    // ... your dev dependencies ...\n  },\n  \"dependencies\": {\n    // \"tslib\": \"^2.x.x\" // tslib is often a runtime dependency when using --importHelpers in tsconfig or by some TS features\n  }\n}\n&#96;\n\n**Publishing Steps:**\n\n1. Ensure your code is committed and pushed to your Git repository.\n2. Build your library: &#96;npm run build&#96; (this should run Rollup and tsc for declarations).\n3. Log in to npm (or your private registry): &#96;npm login&#96;.\n4. Update the version (semantic versioning is recommended):&#96;npm version patch&#96; (for bug fixes: 0.1.0 -\u003e 0.1.1)  \n&#96;npm version minor&#96; (for new features, non-breaking: 0.1.0 -\u003e 0.2.0)  \n&#96;npm version major&#96; (for breaking changes: 0.1.0 -\u003e 1.0.0)\n5. Publish: &#96;npm publish&#96; (add &#96;--access public&#96; if publishing a scoped package to npm for the first time).\n6. Push tags to Git: &#96;git push --tags&#96;.\n\nConsider using tools like &#96;semantic-release&#96; to automate the versioning and publishing process based on commit messages.\n\n## 7\\. Advanced Considerations for Robust Libraries\n\nAs your library grows, consider these advanced topics:\n\n* **Accessibility (A11y):**  \n   * Go beyond basic ARIA attributes. Ensure full keyboard navigability for all interactive components.  \n   * Test with screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS).  \n   * Manage focus states meticulously, especially for modals, dropdowns, and other overlay components.  \n   * Use tools like &#96;@axe-core/react&#96; for automated accessibility checks during development and testing.  \n   * Provide clear documentation on any accessibility implications of your components.\n* **Theming Strategies:**  \n   * **CSS Custom Properties (Variables):** Highly recommended for modern libraries. Define a set of global and component-specific CSS variables for colors, fonts, spacing, etc. Consumers can then override these variables to theme the library.  \n   * **React Context API:** For more dynamic theming or when CSS variables are insufficient (e.g., switching between light/dark mode which might involve more than just CSS). Provide a ThemeProvider component.  \n   * **Styled-components / Emotion Theming:** If using CSS-in-JS, leverage their built-in theming capabilities.  \n   * Document clearly how to apply and customize themes.\n* **Performance Optimization:**  \n   * Use &#96;React.memo&#96; for functional components and &#96;shouldComponentUpdate&#96; (or &#96;PureComponent&#96;) for class components to prevent unnecessary re-renders.  \n   * Memoize expensive calculations with &#96;useMemo&#96; and callbacks with &#96;useCallback&#96;.  \n   * Be mindful of bundle size. Analyze your bundle with tools like &#96;rollup-plugin-visualizer&#96; or &#96;webpack-bundle-analyzer&#96;.  \n   * Lazy load components or parts of your library if they are not immediately needed.  \n   * Ensure efficient event handling and avoid memory leaks.\n* **Developing Utility Hooks \u0026 Data Connectors (Helpers):**  \n   * For internal tools, you might identify common data fetching patterns or interactions with specific internal APIs/databases.  \n   * Create custom hooks (e.g., &#96;useInternalApi(endpoint, options)&#96;) that encapsulate this logic. These hooks are part of your library but are not UI components.  \n   * These hooks can handle loading states, error handling, and data transformation, making it easier for consuming applications to interact with backends consistently.  \n   Copy&#96;&#96; // Example: src/hooks/useQueryData.ts  \n   import { useState, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react';  \n   interface QueryDataOptions {  \n     // Define options: method, headers, body etc.  \n     method?: 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';  \n     headers?: Record\u003cstring, string\u003e;  \n     body?: any;  \n   }  \n   export function useQueryData\u003cT\u003e(url: string, options?: QueryDataOptions) {  \n     const [data, setData] = useState\u003cT | null\u003e(null);  \n     const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);  \n     const [error, setError] = useState\u003cError | null\u003e(null);  \n     const fetchData = useCallback(async () =\u003e {  \n       setLoading(true);  \n       setError(null);  \n       try {  \n         const fetchOptions = {  \n           method: options?.method || 'GET',  \n           headers: {  \n             'Content-Type': 'application/json',  \n             ...options?.headers,  \n           },  \n           body: options?.body ? JSON.stringify(options.body) : undefined,  \n         };  \n         // Replace with your actual fetch logic, error handling, auth etc.  \n         const response = await fetch(url, fetchOptions);  \n         if (!response.ok) {  \n           throw new Error(&#96;HTTP error! status: ${response.status}&#96;);  \n         }  \n         const result = await response.json();  \n         setData(result);  \n       } catch (e) {  \n         setError(e as Error);  \n       } finally {  \n         setLoading(false);  \n       }  \n     }, [url, options]); // Consider options dependency carefully if it's not stable  \n     useEffect(() =\u003e {  \n       fetchData();  \n     }, [fetchData]); // Re-run if fetchData changes (due to url/options change)  \n     return { data, loading, error, refetch: fetchData };  \n   }  \n    &#96;&#96;\n* **Contribution Guidelines \u0026 Code Review:**  \n   * If multiple engineers contribute, establish clear guidelines: coding style (use Prettier and ESLint), commit message conventions, branching strategy (e.g., Gitflow), and PR process.  \n   * Enforce code reviews to maintain quality, share knowledge, and ensure consistency.  \n   * Automate checks with linters and formatters in your CI pipeline.\n* **Internationalization (i18n) and Localization (l10n):**  \n   * If your internal tools need to support multiple languages, plan for i18n from the start. This might involve passing locale props or using a context-based i18n library.\n* **Visual Regression Testing:**  \n   * Tools like Chromatic (by Storybook maintainers), Percy, or Applitools can help catch unintended visual changes in your components.\n\n## 8\\. Conclusion \u0026 Best Practices\n\nBuilding a high-quality **React component library** is an iterative process that requires careful planning, robust tooling, and a commitment to best practices. As an engineer, your focus should be on:\n\n* **Component Design:** Create flexible, composable, and accessible components with clear APIs.\n* **Code Quality:** Write clean, maintainable, and well-typed TypeScript code.\n* **Thorough Testing:** Implement comprehensive unit, integration, and potentially visual regression tests.\n* **Excellent Documentation:** Use Storybook effectively to provide interactive examples and clear usage guidelines. Engineers are key contributors to good documentation.\n* **Collaboration:** If working in a team, follow established contribution guidelines and participate actively in code reviews.\n* **Continuous Improvement:** Regularly revisit and refactor components, optimize for performance, and incorporate feedback from users of the library.\n\nA well-crafted component library will significantly improve the efficiency, consistency, and quality of your organization's internal tools, making it a valuable asset for the engineering team.\n\nDinesh Kumar, VP Engineering, Yubi Group \n\n### \"We didnt build our library for internal tools; we rather used DronaHQ low code platform!\"\n\n \"Building and maintaining our own React component library was a huge time sink. We switched to **DronaHQ**, a visual dev tool, and it's made building internal tools **10x simpler and faster** for our entire engineering team. Now we focus on solving business problems, not UI plumbing.\"\n\n Dinesh Kumar\n\n VP Engineering, Yubi Group\n\n Simplify Your Internal Tooling → ",

Report Abuse \n\nCover image for Building and Documenting UI Components with Storybook and React \n\nDebajit Mallick \n\nDebajit Mallick \n\n Posted on Mar 23 \n\n#  Building and Documenting UI Components with Storybook and React\n\n#react #storybook #frontend #documentation \n\n##  Introduction\n\nHave you ever struggled with maintaining consistency across your UI components or found it challenging to collaborate with designers? I've been there too. After experimenting with several tools, I discovered that Storybook changed my development workflow for the better.\n\nIn this post, I'll walk you through setting up Storybook in a React project and show you how to build and document components that you can reuse throughout your applications.\n\n##  What is Storybook?\n\nIt lets you build and test UI components in isolation, away from the complexity of the full app. The interactive documentation makes it easier for team members to understand how components work. Using Storybook, Setting up visual regression tests became surprisingly simple\n\n##  Getting Started: Project Setup\n\nLet's start by creating our project foundation. Fire up your terminal and run:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm create vite@latest my-storybook-app -- --template react-ts\ncd my-storybook-app\nnpm install\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nWith our React project ready, let's add Storybook to the mix:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook@latest init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis command works like magic – it automatically configures Storybook for your Vite setup, creates a &#96;.storybook/&#96; folder, and adds some example stories in &#96;src/stories/&#96;. Take a moment to explore these files to get familiar with the structure.\n\n##  Creating Our First Component: The Button\n\nLet's start by building a flexible Button component that we can reuse across our application.\n\nFirst, create the component file:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Button.tsx\nimport React from 'react';\n\nexport interface ButtonProps {\n  label: string;\n  onClick?: () =\u003e void;\n  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary';\n}\n\nexport const Button: React.FC\u003cButtonProps\u003e = ({\n  label,\n  onClick,\n  variant = 'primary',\n}) =\u003e {\n  const styles = {\n    primary: 'bg-blue-500 text-white',\n    secondary: 'bg-gray-200 text-black',\n  };\n\n  return (\n    \u003cbutton\n      className={&#96;px-4 py-2 rounded ${styles[variant]}&#96;}\n      onClick={onClick}\n    \u003e\n      {label}\n    \u003c/button\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nNow for the fun part – creating stories for our Button:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Button.stories.tsx\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Button\u003e = {\n  title: 'Components/Button',\n  component: Button,\n};\n\nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Button\u003e;\n\nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    label: 'Click Me',\n    variant: 'primary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Secondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    label: 'Cancel',\n    variant: 'secondary',\n  },\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n##  Building a Card Component\n\nNow that we have our Button, let's create a Card component that can even incorporate our Button.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Card.tsx\nimport React from 'react';\n\nexport interface CardProps {\n  title: string;\n  description: string;\n  children?: React.ReactNode;\n}\n\nexport const Card: React.FC\u003cCardProps\u003e = ({ title, description, children }) =\u003e {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"border rounded-lg shadow-md p-4 max-w-sm\"\u003e\n      \u003ch3 className=\"text-lg font-bold mb-2\"\u003e{title}\u003c/h3\u003e\n      \u003cp className=\"text-gray-700 mb-4\"\u003e{description}\u003c/p\u003e\n      {children}\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nAnd here's how we can showcase it in Storybook:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Card.stories.tsx\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Card } from './Card';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Card\u003e = {\n  title: 'Components/Card',\n  component: Card,\n};\n\nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Card\u003e;\n\nexport const Default: Story = {\n  args: {\n    title: 'Welcome!',\n    description: 'This is a sample card component.',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const WithButton: Story = {\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003cCard {...args}\u003e\n      \u003cButton label=\"Learn More\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/Card\u003e\n  ),\n  args: {\n    title: 'Interactive Card',\n    description: 'This card includes a button as a child component.',\n  },\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nI particularly love this example because it shows how components can be nested in Storybook stories, helping you visualize complex component relationships.\n\n##  Adding Some Style with Tailwind (Optional)\n\nIf you're like me and prefer Tailwind for styling, it's super easy to add:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install -D tailwindcss postcss autoprefixer\nnpx tailwindcss init -p\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nUpdate your CSS with:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n/* in index.css */\n@tailwind base;\n@tailwind components;\n@tailwind utilities;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nDon't forget to add your source folder to the content paths in &#96;tailwind.config.js&#96;!\n\n##  Time to See It in Action!\n\nLet's fire up Storybook and see our components:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nWhen you visit \u003chttp://localhost:6006/\u003e, you'll see your Button and Card components displayed in the Storybook UI. Try clicking around and interacting with different props – it's incredibly satisfying to see your components respond in real-time.\n\n##  Sharing Your Component Library\n\nWant to share your beautiful components with the team or showcase them in a portfolio? Generate a static build:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run build-storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis creates a &#96;storybook-static/&#96; directory that you can deploy to Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages, or any static hosting provider. I've found this especially useful when working with remote teams.\n\n##  Conclusion\n\nUsing Storybook you can develop a consistent design system. Which helps you to onboard new team members more quickly, catch UI bugs before they reach production. Also, you can Communicate more effectively with designers. If you like this blog and want to learn more about **Frontend Development** and **Software Engineering**, you can follow me on Dev.to.\n\n##  Top comments (0) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCode of Conduct • Report abuse \n\n Are you sure you want to hide this comment?       "chunk": "Select ThemeSystem modeDark modeLight mode\n\n* blog\n* dev bites\n* observatory\n\n# Storybook Testing Overview\n\n## Why Storybook ?\n\nWhen you’re building a design system library—or any large UI project—there’s a good chance you’re already using Storybook. There are many reasons for that, mainly:\n\n* great collaboration tool, that showcases UI to stakeholders and other team members early\n* ability to display the component in any state needed in the browser\n* free, interactive docs for the components\n* allow devs to build components in isolation (Visual TDD)\n* straightforward deployment\n* optional integration with their SaaS Chromatic - for automating the visual tests\n\n## Component Tests in Storybook\n\nA few assumptions need to be made:\n\n* project already has setup for Vitest and React testing Library\n* project already has setup for Storybook\n\n### Storybook component tests internals\n\n1. Each story has a &#96;play&#96; function that runs after the component is rendered. It allows simulating user behavior similar to &#96;userEvent&#96; in RTL .\n2. Inside of the each &#96;play&#96; function, you have access to well known assertions, and utilities from the RTL and Vitest. It is part of the &#96;@storybook/test&#96; package.\n3. Each &#96;play&#96; function is executed by a dedicated test runner based on Jest and Playwright.\n4. Finally, &#96;@storybook/addon-interactions&#96; lets us visualize the test in the story and provides a playback mechanism (similar to Cypress/Playwright).\n\nTest runner verifies stories **without** the &#96;play&#96; function for rendering without errors\n\nIn case you need to perform something **before** running the tests test-hook-api got you covered\n\n### \n\nInitial setup\n\n1. Install dependencies &#96;pnpm add --save-dev @storybook/test @storybook/addon-interactions&#96;\n2. In &#96;.storybook/main.ts&#96;, add a new entry to the addons array:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nconst config: StorybookConfig = {\n  // rest of your config\n  addons: [\n    // rest of your config\n    '@storybook/addon-interactions',\n  ],\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Open the storybook &#96;pnpm run storybook&#96;\n2. Add example test based on the &#96;play&#96; function e.g.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nimport { userEvent, within, expect, screen } from '@storybook/test'\n\nexport const SwitchLanguageToSpanish: Story = {\n  play: async () =\u003e {\n    const canvas = within(document.body)\n\n    const select = canvas.getByRole('textbox')\n    expect(select).toHaveValue('EN')\n    expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/\\bES\\b/i)).toBe(null)\n\n    await userEvent.click(select)\n    await userEvent.click(screen.getByText(/\\bES\\b/i))\n\n    await expect(select).toHaveValue('ES')\n    await expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/EN/i)).toBe(null)\n  },\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Run the test in the Storybook UI under the interactions tab inside of the story\n\nExample of running the tests inside of the Storybook UI\n\nInteractions tests Storybook tab\n\n### Example test breakdown\n\nLet's break down the example test from the initial-setup step.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nimport { userEvent, within, expect, screen } from '@storybook/test'\n\nexport const SwitchLanguageToSpanish: Story = {\n  play: async () =\u003e {\n    const canvas = within(document.body)\n    const user = userEvent.setup()\n\n    const select = canvas.getByRole('textbox')\n    expect(select).toHaveValue('EN')\n    expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/\\bES\\b/i)).toBe(null)\n\n    await user.click(select)\n    await user.click(screen.getByText(/\\bES\\b/i))\n\n    expect(select).toHaveValue('ES')\n    expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/EN/i)).toBe(null)\n  },\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. We import RTL like functions and expect from the &#96;@storybook/test&#96;  \nTypeScript won't show missing expect if you are using Vitest or Jest with globals (when you don't have to import it, describe, expect etc.)\n2. Next we define our canvas, think of it as wrapper element of the test container We target the &#96;document.body&#96; because the dropdown is rendered by default in React.Portal\n3. User action is handled like in the RTL by userEvent\n4. Assertions work exactly the same as in regular tests; they’re just imported from &#96;@storybook/test&#96; instead.\n\nProviders (Router, UI Library, etc.) are setup in the Storybook decorators.\n\nComparing it to the RTL version - will demonstrate the many similarities\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\nimport { screen } from \"@testing-library/react\";\n\nimport { LanguageSwitcher } from \"./LanguageSwitcher\";\n\nexport const createUIWrapper = ({ children }: PropsWithChildren) =\u003e {\n\tconst user = userEvent.setup();\n\n\tconst { rerender, unmount, asFragment, baseElement } = render(\n\t\t\u003cUIProviders\u003e{children}\u003c/UIProviders\u003e\n\t);\n\n\treturn {\n\t\tuser,\n\t\trerender,\n\t\tunmount,\n\t\tasFragment,\n\t\tbaseElement,\n\t};\n};\n\ndescribe(\"LanguageSwitcher\", () =\u003e {\n\tit(\"should switch the language\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\tconst { user } = createUIWrapper({ children: \u003cLanguageSwitcher /\u003e });\n\t\tconst select = screen.getByRole(\"textbox\");\n\t\texpect(select).toHaveValue(\"EN\");\n\t\texpect(screen.queryByDisplayValue(/\\bES\\b/i)).toBe(null);\n\n\t\tawait user.click(select);\n\t\tawait user.click(screen.getByText(/\\bES\\b/i));\n\n\t\texpect(select).toHaveValue(\"ES\");\n\t\texpect(screen.queryByDisplayValue(/EN/i)).toBe(null);\n\t});\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Example test with HTTP request\n\nAPI mocking can be achieved with the msw library. We need to install dependencies:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm add -D msw msw-storybook-addon\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nRegister it in the Storybook and init msw\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\n// .storybook/preview.ts\nimport type { Preview } from \"@storybook/react\";\nimport { initialize as initializeMsw, mswLoader } from \"msw-storybook-addon\";\n\ninitializeMsw({ onUnhandledRequest: \"warn\" });\n\nconst preview: Preview = {\n\t// rest of your setup\n\n\tloaders: [mswLoader],\n};\n\nexport default preview;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn my example app I need to mock endpoint &#96;/api/user&#96; to fetch data for profile of 3 different user-roles. This setup will demonstrate the different scenarios.\n\nScenarios, 3 are positives and one is for server failure\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\ntype UserScenario = \"employee\" | \"reseller\" | \"enterprise\" | \"apiError\";\n\nconst scenarioHandlers: Record\u003cUserScenario, () =\u003e HttpResponse\u003e = {\n\temployee: () =\u003e HttpResponse.json(employeeUserFixture),\n\treseller: () =\u003e HttpResponse.json(resellerUserFixture),\n\tenterprise: () =\u003e HttpResponse.json(enterpriseUserFixture),\n\tapiError: () =\u003e\n\t\tnew HttpResponse(\"Internal Server Error\", {\n\t\t\tstatus: 500,\n\t\t\theaders: {\n\t\t\t\t\"Content-Type\": \"text/plain\",\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t}),\n};\n\nexport function createUserProfileHandler(scenario: UserScenario = \"employee\") {\n\treturn http.get(&#96;${apiUrlConfig.baseUrl}${apiUrlConfig.userEndpoint}&#96;, () =\u003e {\n\t\treturn scenarioHandlers[scenario]();\n\t});\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThen all we need to do is use handlers in &#96;parameters.msw&#96; field of the Story\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nexport const Employee: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"employee\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst department = await canvas.findByText(/sales/i);\n\t\tconst managerName = await canvas.findByText(/alice boss/i);\n\n\t\texpect(department).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(managerName).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\nexport const Reseller: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"reseller\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst name = await canvas.findByText(/acme inc./i);\n\t\tconst tier = await canvas.findByText(/silver/i);\n\t\texpect(name).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(tier).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\nexport const Enterprise: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"enterprise\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst supportEmail = await canvas.findByText(/support@global.com/i);\n\n\t\texpect(supportEmail).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\nexport const ErrorState: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"apiError\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst errorInfo = await canvas.findByText(/an error has occurred: HTTP error! status: 500/i);\n\n\t\texpect(errorInfo).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhile the tests are extremely oversimplified, the idea remain the same for more real world scenarios.  \nHere is RTL version of the same test case:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\ndescribe(\"UserProfile\", () =\u003e {\n\tit(\"should display department and manager name when the current user is an employee\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst department = await screen.findByText(/sales/i);\n\t\tconst managerName = await screen.findByText(/alice boss/i);\n\n\t\texpect(department).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(managerName).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n\n\tit(\"should display reseller name and tier when the current user is an reseller\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\ttestServer.use(createUserProfileHandler(\"reseller\"));\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst name = await screen.findByText(/acme inc./i);\n\t\tconst tier = await screen.findByText(/silver/i);\n\n\t\texpect(name).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(tier).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n\n\tit(\"should display a dedicated support email when the current user is an enterprise\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\ttestServer.use(createUserProfileHandler(\"enterprise\"));\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst supportEmail = await screen.findByText(/support@global.com/i);\n\n\t\texpect(supportEmail).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n\n\tit(\"should display an error message on server failure\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\ttestServer.use(createUserProfileHandler(\"apiError\"));\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst errorInfo = await screen.findByText(\n\t\t\t/an error has occurred: HTTP error! status: 500/i\n\t\t);\n\n\t\texpect(errorInfo).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Headless mode\n\nRunning tests with the visual representation is great in the development. However you might also need to run it in the terminal.  \nWe need to add standalone test-runner by installing it:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm add --save-dev @storybook/test-runner concurrently http-server wait-on\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nAdd it to your &#96;package.json&#96; scripts:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;json\n\"scripts\": {\n\t// rest\n\t\"test:ui\": \"test-storybook\",\n\t\"test:ui:ci\": \"concurrently -k -s first -n \\\"STORYBOOK,TEST\\\" \\\"http-server storybook-static --port 6006 --silent\\\" \\\"wait-on tcp:127.0.0.1:6006 \u0026\u0026 time pnpm run test:ui\\\"\"\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe &#96;test:ui&#96; expects already running storybook.  \nTo make sure there is always storybook available in the Github Action we need few more steps:\n\n1. create production build of the Storybook\n2. using &#96;concurrently&#96; package spin off the http-server with production build of the storybook\n3. additionally STORYBOOK and TEST labels are added for processes\n4. run the test:ui command with time unix command to measure its execution time\n\nFull log for this part of github action looks like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\n[TEST] \u003e storybook-testing-playground@0.0.0 test:ui /home/runner/work/storybook-testing-playground/storybook-testing-playground\n[TEST] \u003e test-storybook\n[TEST] \n[TEST] (node:5211) [DEP0040] DeprecationWarning: The &#96;punycode&#96; module is deprecated. Please use a userland alternative instead.\n[TEST] (Use &#96;node --trace-deprecation ...&#96; to show where the warning was created)\n[STORYBOOK] (node:5168) [DEP0066] DeprecationWarning: OutgoingMessage.prototype._headers is deprecated\n[STORYBOOK] (Use &#96;node --trace-deprecation ...&#96; to show where the warning was created)\n[TEST] PASS browser: chromium src/ui/molecules/languageSwitcher/LanguageSwitcher.stories.ts\n[TEST]   molecules/LanguageSwitcher\n[TEST]     DefaultLanguage\n[TEST]       ✓ play-test (85 ms)\n[TEST]     SwitchLanguageToSpanish\n[TEST]       ✓ play-test (52 ms)\n[TEST] \n[TEST] Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total\n[TEST] Tests:       2 passed, 2 total\n[TEST] Snapshots:   0 total\n[TEST] Time:        1.336 wait-on tcp:127.0.0.1:6006 \u0026\u0026 time pnpm run test:ui exited with code 0\n--\u003e Sending SIGTERM to other processes..\n[STORYBOOK] http-server storybook-static --port 6006 --silent exited with code SIGTERM\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### CI Timing overview\n\nAnalyze the results with grain of the salt, since there are only 2 tests in example app. The github-action contains following steps:\n\n* setup pnpm\n* install project deps\n* cache playwright binaries\n* install playwright os-level dependencies\n* run linter\n* run project build\n* run storybook build (needed for our UI tests)\n* run regular unit tests Vitest and RTL\n* run UI tests in storybook using headless mode\n\nBrowser tests using Storybook take almost 5 seconds on CI:  \n&#96;real 0m4.818s&#96; Source: job  \nIn contrast, the same tests written in RTL (happy-dom) take almost 3 seconds on CI:  \n&#96;real 0m2.723s&#96; Source: job\n\nFull github-action:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\nname: Build\non:\n  push:\n    branches: [ main ]\n  pull_request:\n    branches: [ main ]\n\njobs:\n  build:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04\n    strategy:\n      matrix:\n        node-version: [22]\n    steps:\n    - uses: actions/checkout@v4\n    - name: Install pnpm\n      uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4\n      with:\n        version: 9\n    - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}\n      uses: actions/setup-node@v4\n      with:\n        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}\n        cache: 'pnpm'\n    - name: Install dependencies\n      run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile\n    - name: Cache Playwright binaries\n      uses: actions/cache@v4\n      id: playwright-cache\n      with:\n        path: |\n            ~/.cache/ms-playwright\n        key: ${{ runner.os }}-playwright-${{ env.PLAYWRIGHT_VERSION }}\n\n    - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps\n      if: steps.playwright-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'\n\n    - run: pnpm exec playwright install-deps\n    - name: Run linter\n      run: pnpm run lint\n    - name: Run build\n      run: pnpm run build\n    - name: Build Storybook\n      run: pnpm run build-storybook\n    - name: Run unit tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:unit\n    - name: Run browser tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:ui:ci\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Gathering test coverage capabilities\n\nIf you need to chase the coverage in your organization, Storybook provides a way to include it as well for tools like SonarQube.  \nStorybook provides the instrumentation with Istanbul and generates the coverage in the terminal in the following format:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n-----------------------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------\nFile                               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines | Uncovered Line #s\n-----------------------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------\nAll files                          |   93.75 |        0 |   91.66 |   92.59 |\n src                               |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  AppProviders.tsx                 |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/i18n                          |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  LocaleProvider.tsx               |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  useLocale.ts                     |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/i18n/context                  |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  LocaleContext.ts                 |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/i18n/hooks                    |    87.5 |        0 |     100 |    87.5 |\n  useCurrentLocale.ts              |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  useLocaleContext.ts              |      80 |        0 |     100 |      80 | 8\n src/i18n/messages                 |   66.66 |      100 |       0 |   66.66 |\n  messages.ts                      |   66.66 |      100 |       0 |   66.66 | 12\n src/ui/atoms/select               |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  Select.tsx                       |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/ui/molecules/languageSwitcher |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  LanguageSwitcher.tsx             |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n-----------------------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIt creates the &#96;coverage/storybook&#96; folder with common &#96;lcov.info&#96; file for the SonarQube.  \nAdditional configuration for the coverage needs to be done in the &#96;.storybook/main.ts&#96; addon config\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nconst config = {\n  istanbul: {\n    include: ['src/**/stories/**'],\n  },\n};\n\naddons: [\n    // Other Storybook addons setup\n    {\n      name: '@storybook/addon-coverage',\n      options: config,\n    },\n],\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Summary\n\n**Limitations**:\n\n* testing is tied to the Storybook\n* slower than RTL because of:  \n   * need to install the Playwright on CI  \n   * starting the storybook to perform the tests  \n   * running it in the real browser\n* no easy control over versions of Playwright or Vitest used in the &#96;@storybook/test&#96;\n* shockingly there is no way to set test name yet \u003chttps://github.com/storybookjs/test-runner/issues/71\u003e\n\n**Pros**:\n\n* visual debugging in the browser (with playback mechanism)\n* extensibility for a11y test by adding another addon &#96;@storybook/addon-a11y&#96; (based on axe-core)\n* RTL syntax with helpful matchers like &#96;inTheDocument()&#96; or &#96;isVisible()&#96;\n* runs in a real browser, not a synthetic &#96;JSDOM&#96; environment.\n* the errors are logged also in the browser console\n\n**Problems**:\n\n* using vitest global:true collides with Storybook imports like: &#96;import { expect } from \"@storybook/test\";&#96;  \n   * you will get an error in the browser console: &#96;ReferenceError: expect is not defined&#96;, which can be hard to diagnose\n* for pnpm users, you must install Playwright, which the docs currently don't mention:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm exec playwright install\n ERR_PNPM_RECURSIVE_EXEC_FIRST_FAIL  Command \"playwright\" not found\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n* for pnpm CI section in the docs is incomplete - I had to add setup for the Playwright in github-action:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\n    - name: Cache Playwright binaries\n      uses: actions/cache@v4\n      id: playwright-cache\n      with:\n        path: |\n            ~/.cache/ms-playwright\n        key: ${{ runner.os }}-playwright-${{ env.PLAYWRIGHT_VERSION }}\n\n    - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps\n      if: steps.playwright-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'\n    - name: Build Storybook\n      run: pnpm run build-storybook\n    - name: Run unit tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:unit\n    - name: Run browser tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:ui:ci\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n* there are still issues with msw addon integration when using multiple handlers in one story file  \n**Potential great use cases**:\n\nStorybook testing in my opinion, works best for design systems and component libraries. These projects already use Storybook, so adding tests requires minimal extra setup.\n\n© 2025 All rights reserved.",

Inferred Migration\n\n1. Technologies\n2. Test Tools\n3. Storybook\n4. Guides\n5. Storybook best practices for making the most out of Nx\n\n# Storybook best practices for making the most out of Nx\n\n## Purpose of this guide\n\nThe purpose of this guide is to help you set up Storybook in your Nx workspace so that you can get the most out of Nx and its powerful capabilities.\n\n## When to use Storybook\n\nUsually, Storybook is mainly used for two reasons. Testing and documentation. You can read more on when and why to use Storybook in the Why Storybook in 2022? article and also in the Introduction to Storybook documentation page.\n\n### Testing\n\nStorybook helps you test your UIs. You can read more about testing with Storybook in the How to test your UIs with Storybook documentation page. Essentially, Storybook uses the stories as a starting point for testing.\n\n### Documentation\n\nStorybook helps you document your UI elements, or your design system, effectively and in an interactive way. You can read more in the How to document components documentation page. Essentially, you can use Storybook to publish a catalog of your components. A catalog that you can share with the design team, the developer team, the product team, anyone else in the product development process, or even the client. The components are isolated, interactive, and can be represented in all possible forms that they can take (e.g. for a button: enabled, disabled, active, etc). You can read more about publishing your Storybook in the Publish Storybook documentation page.\n\n## Nx and Storybook\n\nNow let’s see how Nx can be used to accommodate both of these pillars of Storybook. Nx takes lots of the burden off your arms when setting up Storybook initially. It essentially provides you with all that you need to start using Storybook’s capabilities (testing and documentation) right away, without having to write a single line of code.\n\n### Development tools\n\nFirst, let’s see what Nx offers, when you are in the process of developing a project with Storybook.\n\n#### Configuration generation\n\nYou can generate the Storybook configuration files and settings using the Nx @nx/storybook:configuration generator. You can read more about configuring Storybook with Nx in our @nx/storybook introduction page. With Nx, you configure Storybook for each individual project.\n\n#### Stories generation\n\nIf you are on a project using Angular, React or React Native, you can also generate stories for your components. You can do so either by using each package's &#96;storybook-configuration&#96; generators or by using the &#96;stories&#96; generator, if you already have Storybook configured for your project.\n\nIf your project is not configured yet, check out one of these guides:\n\n* Set up Storybook for React (and Next.js) Projects\n* Set up Storybook for Angular Projects\n* Set up Storybook for Vue Projects\n\nIf your project is already configured, you can use the &#96;stories&#96; generator:\n\n* React (and Next.js) stories generator\n* Angular stories generator\n* Vue stories generator\n\nThe stories generator will read your inputs (if you’re using Angular), or your props (if you're using React), and will generate stories with the corresponding arguments/controls already prefilled.\n\n#### Storybook interaction tests\n\nStorybook interaction tests allow you to test user interactions within your Storybook stories. It enhances your Storybook setup, ensuring that not only do your components look right, but they also work correctly when interacted with.\n\nNx will generate interaction tests for your stories. You can read more in our Setting up Storybook Interaction Tests with Nx guide.\n\n### CI/CD tools\n\nNow let’s see how Nx helps in the CI/CD journey, as well.\n\n#### Interaction tests in your CI\n\nYou can set up your interaction tests to run as part of your CI. You can read more in the Storybook docs.\n\n#### Serve\n\nWhen you are configuring Storybook, Nx adds a serve and a build target for Storybook in your &#96;project.json&#96;, as we explained above. You can use these targets to serve and build storybook locally, and also in production. Cypress will also use these targets when firing up the e2e tests. While developing, you can serve your Storybooks locally to see if your components work and look as expected. This can help you and speed up the development and debugging process (no need to fire up a complex dev stack).\n\n#### Build and deploy\n\nThe build and deploy step usually comes in handy when you are ready to use Storybook for documentation, and you want to publish it. The building step of Storybook is integrated in the Nx ecosystem, as explained above, and you can trigger your Storybook builds as you would trigger any other build inside your workspace.\n\nWhen you publish your organization’s Storybook, as a result, ideally, you would want to have one shareable Storybook page/application living under one URL, that you can share. With Nx, you can build your Storybook and it will be ready for deployment. **However**, at this point, you have one Storybook per project in your workspace, and you could end up with far too many Storybooks that are built and ready for deployment. This is not ideal, and does not accomplish the ultimate goal of “one shareable documentation page”.\n\nIn the following section, we are going to see how to set up Storybook in these cases, to get the most out of Nx.\n\n## How to set up Storybook to get the most out of Nx\n\n### Philosophy\n\nSetting up Storybook on Nx reflects - and takes advantage of - the mental model of Nx. What that means, in essence, is that you still maintain the individual Storybook instances (per project) which you use for testing and local development, but you also keep one extra “container” for publishing, that serves as a single entry point. Let’s see this in more detail.\n\n#### Local development and testing\n\n##### Development and debugging\n\nIn the process of setting up Storybook in your Nx workspace that we described above, you end up with one Storybook instance per project. That way, you can use your project’s Storybook targets to serve, test and build Storybook:\n\n❯\n\nnx storybook my-project\n\nand\n\n❯\n\nnx build-storybook my-project\n\nand\n\n❯\n\nnx test-storybook my-project\n\nThis feature is extremely useful when developing locally. The containerized stories in your Storybook are the only ones that are built/served/tested when you want to debug just one component, or just one library. You don’t have to wait for a huge Storybook containing all your stories in your repository to fire up. You just need to wait for the Storybook of a single project to start. This speeds up the process.\n\n##### Caching, affected, dependency management\n\nSince each Storybook, in this case, is attached to a project, so is the serving of Storybook and the building of Storybook and the e2e tests for that project. That means that Nx is aware of these tasks, so it caches them, it knows when to fetch them from the cache or re-run them according to the affected status of that project. It also knows that project’s dependencies and knows which things to rebuild before each task.\n\n#### Publishing\n\nWhen you are publishing your Storybook, you can follow the principles described in the project size decision page. The general idea is to have one central Storybook container, into which you are going to gather your stories from multiple libraries.\n\nYou can think of the central Storybook container as a grouping of similar-concept or same-scope UI parts of your workspace. In the same way you are scoping libraries, you can group your stories as well.\n\nThen, according to your use-case, you can have one central Storybook for your whole workspace, importing all the stories from all the projects. Alternatively, you can have one Storybook per \"scope\", which imports all the stories from projects the same scope. Or even one Storybook per application, importing all the stories of all the libraries that it is depending on. As you can see, there are many options, and you can choose the one that best suits your needs.\n\nStorybook Composition\n\nIn order to achieve some things mentioned above, you may use Storybook Composition. However, in this case, you would still need to build each project’s Storybook individually, and also deploy it individually. So in the cases where you have multiple projects, Storybook Composition would not be very efficient.\n\nBefore moving on to the examples section, it could be useful to read the Library Types documentation page and the Grouping libraries documentation page. These could help you decide which way fits your use case better.\n\n## Examples / Use cases\n\nYou can check out the following examples (recipes) to see publishing strategies for Storybook in Nx:\n\n* One main Storybook instance for all projects\n* One Storybook instance per scope\n* One main Storybook instance using Storybook Composition\n\n## Conclusion\n\nIn this guide, we have given a direction towards the most efficient way to use Storybook in a Nx workspace, in a way that takes advantage of the all that Nx has to offer. We have covered the different ways to set up Storybook, and publish it, too. We have also covered the different use cases that apply to each of the solutions.\n\nIf you have any questions or suggestions, please feel free to reach out to us on GitHub, and don't hesitate to ask your questions or share your stories in the Official Nx Discord Server.\n\n### Nx \u0026 Storybook documentation\n\nYou can find all Storybook-related Nx documentation in the packages page.\n\n26.5k\n\nGive us a Star!\n\nOn this page\n* Overview\n* Purpose of this guide\n* When to use Storybook\n* Testing\n* Documentation\n* Nx and Storybook\n* Development tools\n* CI/CD tools\n* How to set up Storybook to get the most out of Nx\n* Philosophy\n* Examples / Use cases\n* Conclusion\n* Nx \u0026 Storybook documentation\n\nFeedback\n\nEdit this page\n\nFeedbackEdit this page\n\n## Footer\n\nNx\n\nSmart Repos · Fast Builds\n\nDiscordGitHubXBlueskyYoutubeLinkedInNewsletter\n\nStatusSecurity\n\nTheme \n\nTheme\n\n### Resources\n\n* Blog\n* Youtube\n* Community\n* Customers\n\n### Solutions\n\n* Nx\n* Nx Cloud\n* Nx Enterprise\n\n### Nx Cloud\n\n* App\n* Docs\n* Pricing\n* Terms\n\n### Company\n\n* About us\n* Careers\n* Brands \u0026 Guidelines\n* Contact us\n\n© 2025 made with  by ",
