      "chunk": "The Candid Startup \n\nPosts Topics Projects About Contact \n\n# Hacking TSDoc support into Storybook\n\n## \n\n##  Feb 17, 2025 • Tim Wiegand \n\n« Feb 10, 2025 Front End Feb 24, 2025 » \n\nLast time, I put together a storybook for my InfiniSheet project. There was one outstanding issue.\n\nStorybook Autodocs \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs\n\nThe Autodocs generated interactive reference documentation is riddled with TSDoc markup that Storybook doesn’t understand. Storybook uses source code static analysis to determine the arguments for each component and extract comments. It generally does a decent job, it just needs a little help with the last ten percent.\n\n# TSDoc Markup\n\nMany TSDoc tags are supported, generally the most basic tags shared with JSDoc. This includes the &#96;@param&#96; tag used to document the arguments to the &#96;onScroll&#96; callback handler.\n\nSome tags, like &#96;@defaultValue&#96;, are stripped out and then ignored. This is particularly annoying as the UI has a column for _Default_ that is left unpopulated. Some, including the &#96;@link&#96; and &#96;@group&#96; tags, aren’t understood at all and come through as is.\n\nThere’s also some odd choices when describing the types of props. The &#96;onScroll&#96; handler is given the accurate and detailed &#96;(offset: number, newScrollState: ScrollState) =\u003e void&#96; followed by descriptions of each parameter. However, the &#96;layout&#96; enum is simply described as &#96;union&#96; rather than the more useful &#96;'horizontal'|'vertical'&#96;.\n\n# Addons and Customization\n\nSurely there must be some addon or customization that I can use to fix this. I tried a few internet searches and found nothing. The documentation mentions JSDoc comments in passing in a few places but no details of what’s supported.\n\nThe generated documentation is created from a set of Doc Blocks using a template which you can customize. The Description and Controls doc blocks display descriptions extracted from my TSDoc comments.\n\nYou can customize doc blocks using the Storybook parameters mechanism. Unfortunately, there’s nothing documented that would let me hook in and handle the TSDoc tags myself.\n\nYou can write your own Doc blocks which have access to the annotated component data including args and description. However, it seems like overkill to reimplement the &#96;Controls&#96; UI from scratch just to manipulate the extracted descriptions first.\n\n# Storybook Source Code\n\nI decided to have a look at the source code. The &#96;Controls&#96; block uses an &#96;ArgTypesExtractor&#96; function to extract metadata for each argument. Interestingly, the extractor is passed to it via a &#96;docs.extractArgTypes&#96; parameter.\n\nParameters is a general Storybook system for managing and sharing named metadata across the Storybook ecosystem. More importantly, parameters can be overridden globally or per component or story.\n\nThe &#96;Description&#96; block works in a similar way, using a function passed in via a &#96;docs.extractComponentDescription&#96; parameter.\n\n# Hooking Extraction Functions\n\nIt looks like &#96;null&#96; is an acceptable return type for each function so I can do a quick test to see if I can override them in the &#96;preview.ts&#96; config file.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst preview: Preview = {\n  parameters: {\n    docs: {\n      extractComponentDescription: () =\u003e { return null },\n      extractArgTypes: () =\u003e { return null }\n    }\n  }\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nOn saving, HMR kicks in and Storybook updates itself.\n\nStorybook Autodocs Hooked \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs Hooked\n\nIt works. We have a way in.\n\nNow that I know what I’m looking for, I found a couple of mentions that suggest this is a somewhat supported approach. Some more searching through source code suggests the following type signatures for the functions.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\ntype ArgTypesExtractor = (component: Component) =\u003e StrictArgTypes | null;\ntype ExtractComponentDescription = (component: Component) =\u003e string | null;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n# Logging Extraction Functions\n\nI updated my hooks and logged the &#96;component&#96; object to the console. Here’s the relevant parts.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n{\n  \"__docgenInfo\": {\n    \"description\": \"Virtual Scrolling List\\n\\nAccepts props defined by {@link VirtualListProps}. \\nRefs are forwarded to {@link VirtualListProxy}. \\nYou must pass a single instance of {@link DisplayListItem} as a child.\\n@group Components\",\n    \"displayName\": \"VirtualList\",\n    \"props\": {\n      \"className\": {\n        \"required\": false,\n        \"tsType\": {\n          \"name\": \"string\"\n        },\n        \"description\": \"The &#96;className&#96; applied to the outer container element. Use when styling the entire component.\"\n      },\n      \"children\": {\n        \"required\": true,\n        \"tsType\": {\n          \"name\": \"ReactComponentType\",\n          \"raw\": \"React.ComponentType\u003cDisplayListItemProps\u003e\",\n        },\n        \"description\": \"Component used as a template to render items in the list. Must implement {@link DisplayListItem} interface.\"\n      },\n      \"itemCount\": {\n        \"required\": true,\n        \"tsType\": {\n          \"name\": \"number\"\n        },\n        \"description\": \"Number of items in the list\"\n      },\n      \"itemOffsetMapping\": {\n        \"required\": true,\n        \"tsType\": {\n          \"name\": \"ItemOffsetMapping\"\n        },\n        \"description\": \"Implementation of {@link ItemOffsetMapping} interface that defines size and offset to each item in the list\\n\\nUse {@link useFixedSizeItemOffsetMapping} or {@link useVariableSizeItemOffsetMapping} to create implementations\\nfor common cases.\"\n      },\n      \"onScroll\": {\n        \"required\": false,\n        \"tsType\": {\n          \"name\": \"signature\",\n          \"type\": \"function\",\n          \"raw\": \"(offset: number, newScrollState: ScrollState) =\u003e void\",\n        },\n        \"description\": \"Callback after a scroll event has been processed and state updated but before rendering\\n@param offset - Resulting overall offset. Can be passed to {@link ItemOffsetMapping} to determine top item.\\n@param newScrollState - New {@link ScrollState} that will be used for rendering.\"\n      },\n    }\n  }\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIt looks like it includes everything needed to populate the UI, after I’ve handled the TSDoc tags.\n\n# Returning Fake Data\n\nIt took a while to find a public definition of the &#96;StrictArgTypes&#96; return value. It’s defined in the separate ComponentDriven/csf repo.\n\nBasically, &#96;StrictArgTypes&#96; is the same as Storybook’s documented ArgTypes. Let’s try returning some fake data. The descriptions seem to support Markdown, so let’s test that.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst preview: Preview = {\n  parameters: {\n    docs: {\n      extractComponentDescription: (component) =\u003e { \n        return \"This is a *description* including &#96;Markdown&#96; syntax with [link](https://www.thecandidstartup.org/)\" \n      },\n      extractArgTypes: (component) =\u003e { \n        return {\n          onScroll: {\n            description: \"It may look like an event handler but I'm claiming it's a magic number instead.\",\n            table: {\n              defaultValue: {\n                summary: \"42\"\n              },\n              type: {\n                summary: \"Magic Number\"\n              }\n            }\n          }\n        }\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNow Storybook looks like this.\n\nStorybook Autodocs Overridden \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs Overridden\n\n# Reusing Existing Conversion Code\n\nHow much of the existing conversion code can we reuse rather than rewriting it from scratch? The implementation of &#96;extractArgTypes&#96; that I’m overriding is defined deep inside React framework support and not exported.\n\nMost framework support, including React, makes use of a common docs-tools library which is exported. The code calls &#96;extractComponentProps&#96; from &#96;docs-tools&#96;, performs some React specific “enhancements” and then reformats the data as &#96;StrictArgTypes&#96;.\n\nThe first and last steps are simple enough to replicate. The enhancement process involves a lot of very verbose code spread over multiple modules which, ironically, is dedicated to nicely formatting the default values that &#96;docs-tools&#96; has failed to extract. I won’t need any of that as I can just use the &#96;@defaultValue&#96; tag from my TSDoc comments.\n\n# Logging Extracted Component Props\n\nI logged the returned values from &#96;extractComponentProps&#96; to the console. The format is extremely verbose so I’ll restrict myself to a couple of informative snippets.\n\nThe format is an array of objects, one for each prop. Each object includes a number of keys of which two are relevant to me. The &#96;propDef&#96; key is another object which includes all the processed data in a form that’s mostly compatible with &#96;StrictArgDefs&#96;. The &#96;docgenInfo&#96; key includes the original data from the &#96;component&#96; object.\n\nHere’s what it looks like for the &#96;layout&#96; prop.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n  {\n    \"propDef\": {\n      \"name\": \"layout\",\n      \"type\": {\n        \"summary\": \"union\"\n      },\n      \"required\": false,\n      \"description\": \"Choice of 'vertical' or 'horizontal' layouts\",\n      \"defaultValue\": null,\n      \"sbType\": {\n        \"raw\": \"\\\"horizontal\\\" | \\\"vertical\\\"\",\n        \"name\": \"enum\",\n        \"value\": [\n            \"horizontal\",\n            \"vertical\"\n        ]\n      }\n    },\n    \"docgenInfo\": {\n      \"required\": false,\n      \"tsType\": {\n        \"name\": \"union\",\n        \"raw\": \"\\\"horizontal\\\" | \\\"vertical\\\"\",\n      },\n      \"description\": \"Choice of 'vertical' or 'horizontal' layouts\\n@defaultValue 'vertical'\"\n    }\n  }\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTwo points to notice. First, the original docgen description includes a &#96;@defaultValue&#96; tag which has been stripped out and ignored. Second, &#96;docs-tools&#96; has recognized that this is an &#96;enum&#96;, extracted the allowed values and still decided to summarize the type as &#96;union&#96;.\n\nLet’s look at something more complex. Here’s the &#96;onScroll&#96; handler.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n  {\n    \"propDef\": {\n      \"name\": \"onScroll\",\n      \"type\": {\n          \"summary\": \"(offset: number, newScrollState: ScrollState) =\u003e void\"\n      },\n      \"required\": false,\n      \"description\": \"Callback after a scroll event has been processed and state updated but before rendering\",\n      \"defaultValue\": null,\n      \"sbType\": {\n          \"raw\": \"(offset: number, newScrollState: ScrollState) =\u003e void\",\n          \"name\": \"function\"\n      },\n      \"jsDocTags\": {\n        \"params\": [\n          {\n            \"name\": \"offset\",\n            \"description\": \"Resulting overall offset. Can be passed to {@link ItemOffsetMapping} to determine top item.\"\n          },\n          {\n            \"name\": \"newScrollState\",\n            \"description\": \"New {@link ScrollState} that will be used for rendering.\"\n          }\n        ],\n        \"deprecated\": null,\n        \"returns\": null,\n        \"ignore\": false\n      }\n    },\n    \"docgenInfo\": {\n      \"required\": false,\n      \"tsType\": {\n        \"name\": \"signature\",\n        \"type\": \"function\",\n        \"raw\": \"(offset: number, newScrollState: ScrollState) =\u003e void\",\n      },\n      \"description\": \"Callback after a scroll event has been processed and state updated but before rendering\\n@param offset - Resulting overall offset. Can be passed to {@link ItemOffsetMapping} to determine top item.\\n@param newScrollState - New {@link ScrollState} that will be used for rendering.\"\n    },\n    \"typeSystem\": \"TypeScript\"\n  }\n]\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn this case, &#96;docs-tools&#96; has summarized the type using the &#96;raw&#96; type signature, the opposite approach to what it did with &#96;layout&#96;. The TSDoc &#96;param&#96; tags from the original description have been extracted and returned in a &#96;jsDocTags&#96; object. There’s no mention of &#96;jsDocTags&#96; in the public ArgTypes documentation.\n\n# Returning Extracted Component Props\n\nMy starting point is to return the &#96;docs-tools&#96; extracted data without any enhancements. I can then incrementally improve the output. After condensing the existing code and removing the React specific enhancements I’m left with this.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport type { StrictArgTypes } from 'storybook/internal/types';\nimport type { ArgTypesExtractor, Component } from 'storybook/internal/docs-tools';\nimport { extractComponentProps, \n  extractComponentDescription as baseExtract } from 'storybook/internal/docs-tools';\n\nexport const extractComponentDescription = (component: Component) =\u003e { \n  const description = baseExtract(component);\n  return description;\n};\n\nexport const extractArgTypes: ArgTypesExtractor = (component) =\u003e {\n  const props = extractComponentProps(component, 'props');\n  if (!props)\n    return null;\n\n  return props.reduce((acc: StrictArgTypes, prop) =\u003e {\n    let {name, description, type, sbType, defaultValue, jsDocTags, required} = prop.propDef;\n\n    acc[name] = { name, description, \n      type: { required, ...sbType },\n      table: { \n        type: type ?? undefined,\n        jsDocTags,\n        defaultValue: defaultValue ?? undefined,\n      }\n    }\n    return acc;\n  }, {});\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhich gets us back to where we started, confirming that the React enhancements were doing nothing for me.\n\nStorybook Autodocs without React enhancements \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs without React enhancements\n\nNow we can start changing things.\n\n# Enhanced Types\n\nLet’s start with something simple. I’m going to provide more detail for &#96;enum&#96; and &#96;union&#96; types.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n  if (sbType.name === 'enum' || sbType.name === 'union')\n    type = { summary: sbType.name, detail: sbType.raw };\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nMy first attempt at this put the raw type data in the summary. Annoyingly, the Markdown pipeline in Storybook filters out &#96;|&#96; characters when formatted in the code style used for types. I tried a few ways of escaping them but nothing worked.\n\nWeirdly, putting the raw type data in the detail does work. I convinced myself that this was an overall improvement as large enums would work better in a pop up.\n\nStorybook Autodocs with enhanced enum \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs with enhanced enum\n\n# Supporting TSDoc the Right Way\n\nThe right way to parse TSDoc markup is to use the official TSDoc parsing library. TSDoc comments can use the full power of Markdown and Markdown isn’t a regular language. Regular expressions won’t cut it.\n\nHowever, it seems like overkill for fixing up my simple comments. To use the TSDoc library I’d first need to reformat the description so that it looks like a source code comment. That is, wrapped in &#96;/**&#96; and &#96;*/&#96; with a &#96;*&#96; prefix on each line. Then I’d have to configure the parser to understand the Typedoc custom tags I’m using.\n\nRunning the parser produces an incredibly verbose abstract syntax tree output structure. You make changes by writing transformers that walk over the tree and manipulate the structure. Finally, you need to write a formatter that walks over the structure recombining everything back into a string.\n\nIt turns out that &#96;docs-tools&#96; has already done the equivalent using the &#96;comment-parser&#96; JSDoc parser. This also explains why &#96;@defaultValue&#96; tags are removed. &#96;comment-parser&#96; extracts all the tags it supports, but &#96;docs-tools&#96; doesn’t do anything with &#96;@defaultValue&#96;.\n\nI’m just fixing a few things up, surely a couple of quick regular expressions can’t hurt?\n\n# Default Values\n\nThis should be the simplest case as the tag has already been removed from the description by &#96;docs-tools&#96;. All I have to do is fish any default value out of the original description in docgenInfo. Default value is a block tag and usually gets a line to itself.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n  const result = \n    prop.docgenInfo.description.match(/\\n\\s*@defaultValue\\s+&#96;*([^\\n&#96;]+)&#96;*(\\n|$)/);\n  if (result)\n    defaultValue = { summary: result[1] }\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe regexp looks for a newline followed by optional white space then the &#96;@defaultValue&#96; tag. There’s more white space, then we capture the value until we hit another newline or the end of the string.\n\nTypedoc formats default values using the normal Markdown rules. If you want to use a code style, you have to use the relevant markup. I do this for function defaults.\n\nStorybook appears to always format default values using code styles. If you include the backtick markup it comes through as a literal character. I fixed this in the regular expression by ignoring any backticks that wrap the value.\n\nStorybook Autodocs with default values \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs with default values\n\nUnfortunately, I’d forgotten about this more complex case\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n/**\n * Function that defines the key to use for each item given row and\n * column index and value of {@link DisplayBaseProps.itemData}.\n * @defaultValue\n * &#96;&#96;&#96;ts\n * (rowIndex, columnIndex, _data) =\u003e &#96;${rowIndex}:${columnIndex}&#96;\n * &#96;&#96;&#96;\n */\nitemKey?: (rowIndex: number, columnIndex: number, data: unknown) =\u003e React.Key\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nDefault value is a block tag so includes everything until the start of the next tag or the end of the comment. You can have multiline default values. I had to do it this way because the function definition makes use of backticks and this was the only way of escaping them that worked with Typedoc.\n\nI considered going back to the right way for all of 30 seconds, then changed the definition to remove the backticks.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n /**\n  * @defaultValue &#96;(rowIndex, columnIndex, _data) =\u003e '${rowIndex}:${columnIndex}'&#96;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis code isn’t literally correct but still does its job of explaining what the default &#96;itemKey&#96; function does.\n\nIt turns out that squashing a function definition into the limited space provided for the “Default” column isn’t very readable. If the value string is longer than 15 characters I return it as detail and use &#96;sbType.name&#96; as the summary.\n\nStorybook Autodocs large default as detail \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs large default as detail\n\n# Group Tag\n\nThis is a custom TypeDoc tag that I use to group components together in the generated documentation. There’s no equivalent in Storybook and no need for one as everything in Storybook is a component. All I need to do is strip the tag out.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n  const noGroup = description.replace(/\\n\\s*@group\\s+([^\\n&#96;]+)(\\n|$)/, \"\");\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNo drama. This one just worked.\n\n# Links\n\nMost links in the descriptions are to interfaces and properties of interfaces. The most appropriate default treatment is to format them as code. I may look at adding actual Markdown links when I add Storybook to my published documentation. I could try and cross-link into the Typedoc generated API documentation. Until then, there’s nothing worth linking to.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nfunction replaceLinks(description: string): string {\n  return description.replaceAll(/{@link\\s+([^}]+)}/g, (_substring, p1) =\u003e {\n    const value = p1 as string;\n    return \"&#96;\" + value + \"&#96;\";\n  })\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nI call &#96;replaceLinks&#96; on component, arg and param descriptions. I was surprised to find that Storybook treats param descriptions as simple text rather than Markdown. The backtick markup comes through as is. However, it looks reasonable enough given that I can’t use any form of styling.\n\nStorybook Autodocs Overridden Links \n\n× \n\nStorybook Autodocs Overridden Links\n\nI think the end result is well worth the minimal level of effort that I put in to achieve it.\n\n# Next Time\n\nTime to get this thing published so you can play around with it yourselves.\n\n« Feb 10, 2025 Front End Feb 24, 2025 » ",

I wanted a quick solution that would keep my TypeScript checks happy and my Storybook setup running smoothly. After a bit of trial and error, I discovered a simple fix that anyone can implement.\n\nThank me by sharing on Twitter 🙏\n\n\u003e The inferred type of ‘meta’ cannot be named without a reference to ‘@storybook/test/node\\_modules/@vitest/spy’. This is likely not portable. A type annotation is necessary.\n\n**1\\. Spotting the Problem**  \nI noticed that the error showed up whenever I used the &#96;satisfies Meta\u003ctypeof Kiosk\u003e&#96; approach in my stories. TypeScript decided to infer everything about &#96;meta&#96; in a way that pulled in references to internal types from &#96;@vitest/spy&#96;, which caused unwanted complexity.\n\n**2\\. Removing the Culprit**  \nTo resolve this issue, I removed the &#96;satisfies&#96; syntax. Instead of allowing TypeScript to infer the type in a way that caused the error, I switched to explicitly annotating my &#96;meta&#96; object.\n\n**3\\. Any price and availability information displayed on \\[relevant Amazon Site(s), as applicable\\] at the time of purchase will apply to the purchase of this product.) \n\nTypeScript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst meta = {\n  ...\n} satisfies Meta\u003ctypeof MyComponent\u003e;\u003cbr\u003e\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nwith:\n\nTypeScript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof MyComponent\u003e = {\n  ...\n};\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis direct annotation stopped TypeScript from inferring references to extra types and got rid of the error message.\n\n**Conclusion**  \nBy swapping out &#96;satisfies&#96; for a straightforward type annotation, I resolved the inference issue and kept my Storybook stories functioning as intended. This small change made my setup cleaner and more predictable. Report Abuse \n\nEduardo Henrique Gris \n\nEduardo Henrique Gris \n\n Posted on May 16 \n\n#  Documentation of components in React with TypeScript using Storybook (version 8)\n\n#react #storybook #typescript #webdev \n\n##  Introduction\n\nPortuguese version: Documentação de componentes em React com Typescript usando Storybook (versão 8)\n\nPreviously, I wrote an article about components documentation using storybook when the version was below 8\\. Due to some changes introduced in version 8 and my deeper understanding of the library, I’m now writing an updated version in this article.  \nStorybook is a lib that allows, among other things, the documentation of components in isolation, parallel to the application.  \nIn this article, I will present a way to customize component documentation. I hope this will help bring visibility to some of the options available when using this library. The following steps will be followed:\n\n* setup: storybook configuration\n* stories: definition of the main scenarios for the components to be documented\n* mdx: documentation of the components, incorporating the customizations defined in the stories\n* example: an example of component documentation will be presented\n\nEach component will have its own &#96;mdx&#96; and &#96;stories&#96; file.\n\n##  Setup\n\nTo add storybook to a React application with the initial configurations, you need to run the following command in the terminal: &#96;npx storybook init&#96;.  \nThis command will detect the project’s dependencies and may ask some questions during the process. Some examples:\n\n* whether you're using &#96;webpack&#96; or &#96;vite&#96; in the project\n* whether it's for documentation or testing\n\nIn this case, choose the option that corresponds to your project, and for documentation, specify that when prompted.  \nNote: some libraries use &#96;rollup&#96; instead of &#96;vite&#96; or &#96;webpack&#96;. In a library I use for learning, which uses &#96;rollup&#96;, I chose the &#96;vite&#96; option and it works fine, but you need to add two additional libraries:\n\n&#96;yarn add vite @storybook/builder-vite --dev&#96;\n\n##  Stories\n\nFor each component, a &#96;*.stories.tsx&#96; file will be created, where the most important customization scenarios to be documented will be defined, following this structure:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from \"react\";\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from \"@storybook/react\";\nimport Component from \"./Component\";\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Component\u003e = {\n  title: \"Component\",\n  component: Component,\n  argTypes: {},\n};\n\nexport default meta;\n\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Component\u003e;\n\nexport const Default: Story = {\n  args: {},\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003cComponent {...args} /\u003e\n  ),\n};\n\nexport const Scenario1: Story = {\n  args: {},\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003c\u003e\n      \u003cComponent {...args} /\u003e\n      \u003cComponent {...args} props1=\"option1\" /\u003e\n      \u003cComponent {...args} props1=\"option2\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/\u003e\n  ),\n};\n\n// Scenario2\n// Scenario3\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nFrom the imports of &#96;@storybook/react&#96;:\n\n* Meta: define the metadata for the component to be documented. In this case, the component itself is passed in &#96;component&#96;, and the title that will appear in the sidebar is specified in &#96;title&#96;\n* StoryObj: allows you to define the customization scenarios of the component to be displayed in the documentation, corresponding to the definitions of &#96;Default&#96;, &#96;Scenario1&#96;, &#96;Scenario2&#96;... mentioned above\n\nFor each defined scenario, an entry will be created in the sidebar, within the \"folder\" named according to the &#96;title&#96; defined in the &#96;Meta&#96;, with the following structure:\n\n* Component  \n   * Default  \n   * Scenario 1  \n   * Scenario 2  \n   * Scenario 3\n\nIn &#96;Default&#96;, the component is rendered with its default properties.  \nIn the &#96;args: {}&#96; of &#96;Scenario1&#96; above, no props were passed in, with the goal of showing the component’s base behavior on its initial render using default values.  \nIn the two other renderings inside &#96;Scenario1&#96;, the &#96;props1&#96; prop is varied. The purpose of this scenario is to demonstrate in the documentation what happens to the component when this prop changes.\n\n##  MDX\n\nIt will be the component documentation, where the scenarios present in the &#96;*.stories.tsx&#96; file will be included, and texts will be defined to explain the main functionalities of the component, following this structure:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { Canvas, Controls, Meta, Story } from '@storybook/blocks';\nimport * as Stories from './Component.stories';\n\n\u003cMeta of={Stories} /\u003e\n\n# Component\n\nComponent description.\n\n\u003cCanvas of={Stories.Default} withToolbar /\u003e\n\n\u003cControls of={Stories.Default} /\u003e\n\n## Predefined properties\n\n### Scenario 1\n\nDescription of the use of props1.\n\n\u003cCanvas of={Stories.Scenario1} withToolbar /\u003e\n\n## Custom properties\n\n// ### Scenario 2\n\n// ### Scenario 3\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nIt's a file that mixes markdown with javaScript. From the imports of &#96;@storybook/blocks&#96;:\n\n* Canvas: this will create a box where the components from the scenario defined in the &#96;*.stories&#96; file will be displayed. It includes an option called &#96;Show code&#96; that reveals the code to use the displayed component:\n\nImage description\n\n* Controls: will display a table with the name of all the props available for the component, their descriptions (including the types of the props), whether they have a default value, and a section where you can modify the component's props to see the changes in real time. Putting it all together:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\u003cCanvas of={Stories.Default} withToolbar /\u003e\n\n\u003cControls of={Stories.Default} /\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis sets up Controls to affect the component coming from &#96;Stories.Default&#96;. And above, that component is rendered using &#96;\u003cCanvas of={Stories.Default} withToolbar /\u003e&#96;, so with each prop change, you’ll be able to see how the component gets customized in real time:\n\nImage description\n\n* Meta: defines where the associated stories file for the documentation is located, coming from the import &#96;import * as Stories from './Component.stories';&#96;\n\n##  Example\n\nI will present a simple example of documentation based on what has been provided above. Starting with the creation of a component defined in &#96;Tag.tsx&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from \"react\";\nimport styled from \"styled-components\";\n\nexport interface TagProps {\n  text?: string;\n  backgroundColor?: string;\n  type?: \"default\" | \"success\" | \"alert\" | \"error\";\n}\n\nexport interface StyledTagProps {\n  $backgroundColor?: string;\n  $type?: \"default\" | \"success\" | \"alert\" | \"error\";\n}\n\nexport const StyledTag = styled.div\u003cStyledTagProps\u003e&#96;\n  border: none;\n  padding: 10px 12px;\n  background-color: ${(props) =\u003e\n    props.$backgroundColor\n      ? props.$backgroundColor\n      : props.$type === \"error\"\n        ? \"#e97451\"\n        : props.$type === \"alert\"\n          ? \"#f8de7e\"\n          : props.$type === \"success\"\n            ? \"#50c878\"\n            : props.$type === \"default\"\n            \u0026\u0026 \"#d3d3d3\"};\n  pointer-events: none;\n  border-radius: 5px;\n  width: fit-content;\n&#96;;\n\nconst Tag = ({\n  text=\"Tag\",\n  backgroundColor,\n  type=\"default\",\n}: TagProps) =\u003e (\n  \u003cStyledTag\n    $type={type}\n    $backgroundColor={backgroundColor}\n  \u003e\n    \u003cspan\u003e{text}\u003c/span\u003e\n  \u003c/StyledTag\u003e\n);\n\nexport default Tag;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nIt is a Tag component with a predefined &#96;type&#96; property, meaning that the app itself defines the associated css based on the given type. The possible values are &#96;default&#96;, &#96;error&#96;, &#96;alert&#96; and &#96;success&#96;.  \nIt also has a customizable &#96;backgroundColor&#96; property, allowing users to choose any color they want.  \nIn the example, the css is defined using a lib called &#96;styled-components&#96;, but the documentation is indifferent to how the css is defined. Types are defined for both the component's props and the related to styled component.\n\nNow, a specific component for documentation, &#96;StorybookContainer&#96;, will be created. This component will be responsible for centering the scenario components inside the &#96;Canvas&#96; of the mdx file, with a small spacement between them. In the file &#96;StorybookContainer.tsx&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from \"react\";\nimport styled from \"styled-components\";\n\nexport interface StorybookContainerProps {\n  children: React.ReactNode;\n}\n\nexport const StyledStorybookContainer = styled.div&#96;\n  display: flex;\n  align-items: center;\n  justify-content: center;\n  gap: 10px;\n&#96;;\n\nconst StorybookContainer = ({ children }: StorybookContainerProps) =\u003e (\n  \u003cStyledStorybookContainer\u003e\n    {children}\n  \u003c/StyledStorybookContainer\u003e\n);\n\nexport default StorybookContainer;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThe file &#96;Tag.stories.tsx&#96; will be created with the Default and two scenarios to be presented in the documentation:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from \"react\";\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from \"@storybook/react\";\nimport Tag from \"./Tag\";\nimport StorybookContainer from \"../StorybookContainer/StorybookContainer\";\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Tag\u003e = {\n  title: \"Tag\",\n  component: Tag,\n  argTypes: {},\n};\n\nexport default meta;\n\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Tag\u003e;\n\nexport const Default: Story = {\n  args: {},\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003cStorybookContainer\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} /\u003e\n    \u003c/StorybookContainer\u003e\n  ),\n};\n\nexport const PredefinedType: Story = {\n  args: {},\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003cStorybookContainer\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} /\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} type=\"success\" /\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} type=\"alert\" /\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} type=\"error\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/StorybookContainer\u003e\n  ),\n};\n\nexport const BackgroundColor: Story = {\n  args: {\n    backgroundColor: \"#d3d3d3\",\n  },\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003cStorybookContainer\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} /\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} backgroundColor=\"#89cff0\" /\u003e\n      \u003cTag {...args} backgroundColor=\"#f0aa89\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/StorybookContainer\u003e\n  ),\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nTwo scenarios were defined in the file to show how the component changes with variations in the &#96;type&#96; props (which is a predefined property in the app) and how the component changes with variations in the &#96;backgroundColor&#96; props (which is customizable, as the user can specify any color they want to use).\n\nFinally, the documentation file for the Tag component, &#96;Tag.mdx&#96;, will be created, where the two scenarios defined in the stories file will be displayed:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { Canvas, Controls, Meta } from \"@storybook/blocks\";\nimport * as Stories from \"./Tag.stories\";\n\n\u003cMeta of={Stories} /\u003e\n\n# Tag\n\nTag base component.\n\n\u003cCanvas of={Stories.Default} withToolbar /\u003e\n\n\u003cControls of={Stories.Default} /\u003e\n\n## Predefined properties\n\n### Type\n\nThere are four predefined types: default, success, alert and error.\n\n\u003cCanvas of={Stories.PredefinedType} withToolbar /\u003e\n\n## Custom properties\n\n### Background Color\n\nTag background color can be modified.\n\n\u003cCanvas of={Stories.BackgroundColor} withToolbar /\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis is where the component being displayed will be described, along with a table that allows you to control its props, thanks to the inclusion of &#96;\u003cControls /\u003e&#96;, which appears just above. A customization scenario will be shown by varying the &#96;type&#96; prop (a predefined property), and another scenario will be shown by varying the &#96;backgroundColor&#96; prop (a customizable property).\n\nFinally, run &#96;yarn storybook&#96; in the terminal.  \nThe sidebar will look like this:\n\nImage description\n\nAnd the documentation will look like this:\n\nImage description\n\n##  Conclusion\n\nThe idea of this article was to introduce a component documentation lib that allows customizing documentation using an mdx file in various ways, utilizing the &#96;blocks&#96; provided by the lib. A way for writing this documentation file was presented, but given the many possibilities offered by the lib, I will include some links in the references for those who want to delve deeper into the subject.\n\n##  References\n\nStories File  \nBlocks  \nControls Block  \nCanvas Block  \nMeta Block  \nStories Block  \nMDX File\n\n##  Top comments (0) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCode of Conduct • Report abuse \n\n Are you sure you want to hide this comment?       "chunk": "Select ThemeSystem modeDark modeLight mode\n\n* blog\n* dev bites\n* observatory\n\n# Storybook Testing Overview\n\n## Why Storybook ?\n\nWhen you’re building a design system library—or any large UI project—there’s a good chance you’re already using Storybook. There are many reasons for that, mainly:\n\n* great collaboration tool, that showcases UI to stakeholders and other team members early\n* ability to display the component in any state needed in the browser\n* free, interactive docs for the components\n* allow devs to build components in isolation (Visual TDD)\n* straightforward deployment\n* optional integration with their SaaS Chromatic - for automating the visual tests\n\n## Component Tests in Storybook\n\nA few assumptions need to be made:\n\n* project already has setup for Vitest and React testing Library\n* project already has setup for Storybook\n\n### Storybook component tests internals\n\n1. Each story has a &#96;play&#96; function that runs after the component is rendered. It allows simulating user behavior similar to &#96;userEvent&#96; in RTL .\n2. Inside of the each &#96;play&#96; function, you have access to well known assertions, and utilities from the RTL and Vitest. It is part of the &#96;@storybook/test&#96; package.\n3. Each &#96;play&#96; function is executed by a dedicated test runner based on Jest and Playwright.\n4. Finally, &#96;@storybook/addon-interactions&#96; lets us visualize the test in the story and provides a playback mechanism (similar to Cypress/Playwright).\n\nTest runner verifies stories **without** the &#96;play&#96; function for rendering without errors\n\nIn case you need to perform something **before** running the tests test-hook-api got you covered\n\n### \n\nInitial setup\n\n1. Install dependencies &#96;pnpm add --save-dev @storybook/test @storybook/addon-interactions&#96;\n2. In &#96;.storybook/main.ts&#96;, add a new entry to the addons array:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nconst config: StorybookConfig = {\n  // rest of your config\n  addons: [\n    // rest of your config\n    '@storybook/addon-interactions',\n  ],\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Open the storybook &#96;pnpm run storybook&#96;\n2. Add example test based on the &#96;play&#96; function e.g.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nimport { userEvent, within, expect, screen } from '@storybook/test'\n\nexport const SwitchLanguageToSpanish: Story = {\n  play: async () =\u003e {\n    const canvas = within(document.body)\n\n    const select = canvas.getByRole('textbox')\n    expect(select).toHaveValue('EN')\n    expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/\\bES\\b/i)).toBe(null)\n\n    await userEvent.click(select)\n    await userEvent.click(screen.getByText(/\\bES\\b/i))\n\n    await expect(select).toHaveValue('ES')\n    await expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/EN/i)).toBe(null)\n  },\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Run the test in the Storybook UI under the interactions tab inside of the story\n\nExample of running the tests inside of the Storybook UI\n\nInteractions tests Storybook tab\n\n### Example test breakdown\n\nLet's break down the example test from the initial-setup step.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nimport { userEvent, within, expect, screen } from '@storybook/test'\n\nexport const SwitchLanguageToSpanish: Story = {\n  play: async () =\u003e {\n    const canvas = within(document.body)\n    const user = userEvent.setup()\n\n    const select = canvas.getByRole('textbox')\n    expect(select).toHaveValue('EN')\n    expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/\\bES\\b/i)).toBe(null)\n\n    await user.click(select)\n    await user.click(screen.getByText(/\\bES\\b/i))\n\n    expect(select).toHaveValue('ES')\n    expect(canvas.queryByDisplayValue(/EN/i)).toBe(null)\n  },\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. We import RTL like functions and expect from the &#96;@storybook/test&#96;  \nTypeScript won't show missing expect if you are using Vitest or Jest with globals (when you don't have to import it, describe, expect etc.)\n2. Next we define our canvas, think of it as wrapper element of the test container We target the &#96;document.body&#96; because the dropdown is rendered by default in React.Portal\n3. User action is handled like in the RTL by userEvent\n4. Assertions work exactly the same as in regular tests; they’re just imported from &#96;@storybook/test&#96; instead.\n\nProviders (Router, UI Library, etc.) are setup in the Storybook decorators.\n\nComparing it to the RTL version - will demonstrate the many similarities\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\nimport { screen } from \"@testing-library/react\";\n\nimport { LanguageSwitcher } from \"./LanguageSwitcher\";\n\nexport const createUIWrapper = ({ children }: PropsWithChildren) =\u003e {\n\tconst user = userEvent.setup();\n\n\tconst { rerender, unmount, asFragment, baseElement } = render(\n\t\t\u003cUIProviders\u003e{children}\u003c/UIProviders\u003e\n\t);\n\n\treturn {\n\t\tuser,\n\t\trerender,\n\t\tunmount,\n\t\tasFragment,\n\t\tbaseElement,\n\t};\n};\n\ndescribe(\"LanguageSwitcher\", () =\u003e {\n\tit(\"should switch the language\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\tconst { user } = createUIWrapper({ children: \u003cLanguageSwitcher /\u003e });\n\t\tconst select = screen.getByRole(\"textbox\");\n\t\texpect(select).toHaveValue(\"EN\");\n\t\texpect(screen.queryByDisplayValue(/\\bES\\b/i)).toBe(null);\n\n\t\tawait user.click(select);\n\t\tawait user.click(screen.getByText(/\\bES\\b/i));\n\n\t\texpect(select).toHaveValue(\"ES\");\n\t\texpect(screen.queryByDisplayValue(/EN/i)).toBe(null);\n\t});\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Example test with HTTP request\n\nAPI mocking can be achieved with the msw library. We need to install dependencies:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm add -D msw msw-storybook-addon\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nRegister it in the Storybook and init msw\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\n// .storybook/preview.ts\nimport type { Preview } from \"@storybook/react\";\nimport { initialize as initializeMsw, mswLoader } from \"msw-storybook-addon\";\n\ninitializeMsw({ onUnhandledRequest: \"warn\" });\n\nconst preview: Preview = {\n\t// rest of your setup\n\n\tloaders: [mswLoader],\n};\n\nexport default preview;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn my example app I need to mock endpoint &#96;/api/user&#96; to fetch data for profile of 3 different user-roles. This setup will demonstrate the different scenarios.\n\nScenarios, 3 are positives and one is for server failure\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\ntype UserScenario = \"employee\" | \"reseller\" | \"enterprise\" | \"apiError\";\n\nconst scenarioHandlers: Record\u003cUserScenario, () =\u003e HttpResponse\u003e = {\n\temployee: () =\u003e HttpResponse.json(employeeUserFixture),\n\treseller: () =\u003e HttpResponse.json(resellerUserFixture),\n\tenterprise: () =\u003e HttpResponse.json(enterpriseUserFixture),\n\tapiError: () =\u003e\n\t\tnew HttpResponse(\"Internal Server Error\", {\n\t\t\tstatus: 500,\n\t\t\theaders: {\n\t\t\t\t\"Content-Type\": \"text/plain\",\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t}),\n};\n\nexport function createUserProfileHandler(scenario: UserScenario = \"employee\") {\n\treturn http.get(&#96;${apiUrlConfig.baseUrl}${apiUrlConfig.userEndpoint}&#96;, () =\u003e {\n\t\treturn scenarioHandlers[scenario]();\n\t});\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThen all we need to do is use handlers in &#96;parameters.msw&#96; field of the Story\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nexport const Employee: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"employee\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst department = await canvas.findByText(/sales/i);\n\t\tconst managerName = await canvas.findByText(/alice boss/i);\n\n\t\texpect(department).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(managerName).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\nexport const Reseller: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"reseller\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst name = await canvas.findByText(/acme inc./i);\n\t\tconst tier = await canvas.findByText(/silver/i);\n\t\texpect(name).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(tier).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\nexport const Enterprise: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"enterprise\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst supportEmail = await canvas.findByText(/support@global.com/i);\n\n\t\texpect(supportEmail).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\nexport const ErrorState: StoryObj\u003ctypeof UserProfile\u003e = {\n\tparameters: {\n\t\tmsw: {\n\t\t\thandlers: [createUserProfileHandler(\"apiError\")],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\n\tplay: async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n\t\tconst canvas = within(canvasElement);\n\n\t\tconst errorInfo = await canvas.findByText(/an error has occurred: HTTP error! status: 500/i);\n\n\t\texpect(errorInfo).toBeVisible();\n\t},\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhile the tests are extremely oversimplified, the idea remain the same for more real world scenarios.  \nHere is RTL version of the same test case:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\ndescribe(\"UserProfile\", () =\u003e {\n\tit(\"should display department and manager name when the current user is an employee\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst department = await screen.findByText(/sales/i);\n\t\tconst managerName = await screen.findByText(/alice boss/i);\n\n\t\texpect(department).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(managerName).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n\n\tit(\"should display reseller name and tier when the current user is an reseller\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\ttestServer.use(createUserProfileHandler(\"reseller\"));\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst name = await screen.findByText(/acme inc./i);\n\t\tconst tier = await screen.findByText(/silver/i);\n\n\t\texpect(name).toBeVisible();\n\t\texpect(tier).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n\n\tit(\"should display a dedicated support email when the current user is an enterprise\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\ttestServer.use(createUserProfileHandler(\"enterprise\"));\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst supportEmail = await screen.findByText(/support@global.com/i);\n\n\t\texpect(supportEmail).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n\n\tit(\"should display an error message on server failure\", async () =\u003e {\n\t\ttestServer.use(createUserProfileHandler(\"apiError\"));\n\t\tcreateTestWrapper({ children: \u003cUserProfile /\u003e });\n\n\t\tconst errorInfo = await screen.findByText(\n\t\t\t/an error has occurred: HTTP error! status: 500/i\n\t\t);\n\n\t\texpect(errorInfo).toBeVisible();\n\t});\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Headless mode\n\nRunning tests with the visual representation is great in the development. However you might also need to run it in the terminal.  \nWe need to add standalone test-runner by installing it:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm add --save-dev @storybook/test-runner concurrently http-server wait-on\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nAdd it to your &#96;package.json&#96; scripts:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;json\n\"scripts\": {\n\t// rest\n\t\"test:ui\": \"test-storybook\",\n\t\"test:ui:ci\": \"concurrently -k -s first -n \\\"STORYBOOK,TEST\\\" \\\"http-server storybook-static --port 6006 --silent\\\" \\\"wait-on tcp:127.0.0.1:6006 \u0026\u0026 time pnpm run test:ui\\\"\"\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe &#96;test:ui&#96; expects already running storybook.  \nTo make sure there is always storybook available in the Github Action we need few more steps:\n\n1. create production build of the Storybook\n2. using &#96;concurrently&#96; package spin off the http-server with production build of the storybook\n3. additionally STORYBOOK and TEST labels are added for processes\n4. run the test:ui command with time unix command to measure its execution time\n\nFull log for this part of github action looks like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\n[TEST] \u003e storybook-testing-playground@0.0.0 test:ui /home/runner/work/storybook-testing-playground/storybook-testing-playground\n[TEST] \u003e test-storybook\n[TEST] \n[TEST] (node:5211) [DEP0040] DeprecationWarning: The &#96;punycode&#96; module is deprecated. Please use a userland alternative instead.\n[TEST] (Use &#96;node --trace-deprecation ...&#96; to show where the warning was created)\n[STORYBOOK] (node:5168) [DEP0066] DeprecationWarning: OutgoingMessage.prototype._headers is deprecated\n[STORYBOOK] (Use &#96;node --trace-deprecation ...&#96; to show where the warning was created)\n[TEST] PASS browser: chromium src/ui/molecules/languageSwitcher/LanguageSwitcher.stories.ts\n[TEST]   molecules/LanguageSwitcher\n[TEST]     DefaultLanguage\n[TEST]       ✓ play-test (85 ms)\n[TEST]     SwitchLanguageToSpanish\n[TEST]       ✓ play-test (52 ms)\n[TEST] \n[TEST] Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total\n[TEST] Tests:       2 passed, 2 total\n[TEST] Snapshots:   0 total\n[TEST] Time:        1.336 s\n[TEST] Ran all test suites.\n[TEST] 2.76user 0.55system 0:02.94elapsed 112%CPU (0avgtext+0avgdata 274736maxresident)k\n[TEST] 4200inputs+5560outputs (72major+111257minor)pagefaults 0swaps\n[TEST] wait-on tcp:127.0.0.1:6006 \u0026\u0026 time pnpm run test:ui exited with code 0\n--\u003e Sending SIGTERM to other processes..\n[STORYBOOK] http-server storybook-static --port 6006 --silent exited with code SIGTERM\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### CI Timing overview\n\nAnalyze the results with grain of the salt, since there are only 2 tests in example app. The github-action contains following steps:\n\n* setup pnpm\n* install project deps\n* cache playwright binaries\n* install playwright os-level dependencies\n* run linter\n* run project build\n* run storybook build (needed for our UI tests)\n* run regular unit tests Vitest and RTL\n* run UI tests in storybook using headless mode\n\nBrowser tests using Storybook take almost 5 seconds on CI:  \n&#96;real 0m4.818s&#96; Source: job  \nIn contrast, the same tests written in RTL (happy-dom) take almost 3 seconds on CI:  \n&#96;real 0m2.723s&#96; Source: job\n\nFull github-action:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\nname: Build\non:\n  push:\n    branches: [ main ]\n  pull_request:\n    branches: [ main ]\n\njobs:\n  build:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04\n    strategy:\n      matrix:\n        node-version: [22]\n    steps:\n    - uses: actions/checkout@v4\n    - name: Install pnpm\n      uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4\n      with:\n        version: 9\n    - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}\n      uses: actions/setup-node@v4\n      with:\n        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}\n        cache: 'pnpm'\n    - name: Install dependencies\n      run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile\n    - name: Cache Playwright binaries\n      uses: actions/cache@v4\n      id: playwright-cache\n      with:\n        path: |\n            ~/.cache/ms-playwright\n        key: ${{ runner.os }}-playwright-${{ env.PLAYWRIGHT_VERSION }}\n\n    - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps\n      if: steps.playwright-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'\n\n    - run: pnpm exec playwright install-deps\n    - name: Run linter\n      run: pnpm run lint\n    - name: Run build\n      run: pnpm run build\n    - name: Build Storybook\n      run: pnpm run build-storybook\n    - name: Run unit tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:unit\n    - name: Run browser tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:ui:ci\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Gathering test coverage capabilities\n\nIf you need to chase the coverage in your organization, Storybook provides a way to include it as well for tools like SonarQube.  \nStorybook provides the instrumentation with Istanbul and generates the coverage in the terminal in the following format:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n-----------------------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------\nFile                               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines | Uncovered Line #s\n-----------------------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------\nAll files                          |   93.75 |        0 |   91.66 |   92.59 |\n src                               |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  AppProviders.tsx                 |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/i18n                          |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  LocaleProvider.tsx               |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  useLocale.ts                     |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/i18n/context                  |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  LocaleContext.ts                 |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/i18n/hooks                    |    87.5 |        0 |     100 |    87.5 |\n  useCurrentLocale.ts              |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  useLocaleContext.ts              |      80 |        0 |     100 |      80 | 8\n src/i18n/messages                 |   66.66 |      100 |       0 |   66.66 |\n  messages.ts                      |   66.66 |      100 |       0 |   66.66 | 12\n src/ui/atoms/select               |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  Select.tsx                       |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n src/ui/molecules/languageSwitcher |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n  LanguageSwitcher.tsx             |     100 |      100 |     100 |     100 |\n-----------------------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIt creates the &#96;coverage/storybook&#96; folder with common &#96;lcov.info&#96; file for the SonarQube.  \nAdditional configuration for the coverage needs to be done in the &#96;.storybook/main.ts&#96; addon config\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nconst config = {\n  istanbul: {\n    include: ['src/**/stories/**'],\n  },\n};\n\naddons: [\n    // Other Storybook addons setup\n    {\n      name: '@storybook/addon-coverage',\n      options: config,\n    },\n],\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Summary\n\n**Limitations**:\n\n* testing is tied to the Storybook\n* slower than RTL because of:  \n   * need to install the Playwright on CI  \n   * starting the storybook to perform the tests  \n   * running it in the real browser\n* no easy control over versions of Playwright or Vitest used in the &#96;@storybook/test&#96;\n* shockingly there is no way to set test name yet \u003chttps://github.com/storybookjs/test-runner/issues/71\u003e\n\n**Pros**:\n\n* visual debugging in the browser (with playback mechanism)\n* extensibility for a11y test by adding another addon &#96;@storybook/addon-a11y&#96; (based on axe-core)\n* RTL syntax with helpful matchers like &#96;inTheDocument()&#96; or &#96;isVisible()&#96;\n* runs in a real browser, not a synthetic &#96;JSDOM&#96; environment.\n* the errors are logged also in the browser console\n\n**Problems**:\n\n* using vitest global:true collides with Storybook imports like: &#96;import { expect } from \"@storybook/test\";&#96;  \n   * you will get an error in the browser console: &#96;ReferenceError: expect is not defined&#96;, which can be hard to diagnose\n* for pnpm users, you must install Playwright, which the docs currently don't mention:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm exec playwright install\n ERR_PNPM_RECURSIVE_EXEC_FIRST_FAIL  Command \"playwright\" not found\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n* for pnpm CI section in the docs is incomplete - I had to add setup for the Playwright in github-action:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\n    - name: Cache Playwright binaries\n      uses: actions/cache@v4\n      id: playwright-cache\n      with:\n        path: |\n            ~/.cache/ms-playwright\n        key: ${{ runner.os }}-playwright-${{ env.PLAYWRIGHT_VERSION }}\n\n    - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps\n      if: steps.playwright-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'\n    - name: Build Storybook\n      run: pnpm run build-storybook\n    - name: Run unit tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:unit\n    - name: Run browser tests\n      run: time pnpm run test:ui:ci\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n* there are still issues with msw addon integration when using multiple handlers in one story file  \n**Potential great use cases**:\n\nStorybook testing in my opinion, works best for design systems and component libraries. These projects already use Storybook, so adding tests requires minimal extra setup.\n\n© 2025 All rights reserved.",

Report Abuse \n\nCover image for A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation \n\nAustin Welsh \n\nAustin Welsh \n\n Posted on Feb 17 \n\n#  A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation\n\n#webdev #ui #react #javascript \n\n👋 **Let's Connect!** Follow me on GitHub for new projects.\n\n---\n\n## **Introduction** \n\nBuilding **consistent and scalable UI components** is crucial in modern web development. **Storybook** is a tool that allows developers to **isolate, develop, test, and document UI components** in a sandboxed environment. \n\nStorybook enables you to:  \n  \n✅ **Develop components in isolation** without running a full application.  \n  \n✅ **Create a component library** for design consistency.  \n  \n✅ **Test and document UI behavior** interactively.  \n  \n✅ **Integrate with frameworks like React, Vue, Angular, and more**. \n\nIn this comprehensive guide, we’ll cover: \n\n* **Setting up Storybook**\n* **Writing and organizing stories**\n* **Using add-ons and controls**\n* **Testing components with Storybook**\n* **Mocking API requests**\n* **Visual regression testing**\n* **Automating accessibility testing**\n* **Snapshot testing**\n* **Theming in Storybook**\n* **Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E testing**\n* **Deploying Storybook as documentation**\n* **Best practices for Storybook projects**\n\n---\n\n##  What is Storybook?\n\nStorybook is an open-source tool for **building UI components in isolation**. It provides a dedicated environment for testing and documenting components **without running the entire application**. \n\n### **Why Use Storybook?** \n\n| Feature                                                | Storybook |\n| ------------------------------------------------------ | --------- |\n| Develop components **in isolation**                    | ✅ Yes     |\n| Interactive **component preview**                      | ✅ Yes     |\n| Built-in **documentation generation**                  | ✅ Yes     |\n| Supports **multiple frameworks** (React, Vue, Angular) | ✅ Yes     |\n| Integration with **Jest, Testing Library, Playwright** | ✅ Yes     |\n\n---\n\n##  Installing and Setting Up Storybook\n\nStorybook can be installed in a new or existing project. \n\n### **Installation for React** \n\nRun the following command in your project directory:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook@latest init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Automatically detects the framework and **configures Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ Generates a &#96;.storybook&#96; folder with configuration files.  \n  \n✔ Creates example stories to get started. \n\n### **Starting Storybook** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStorybook will launch on &#96;http://localhost:6006/&#96;.\n\n---\n\n##  Writing Your First Story\n\nA **story** represents a UI component's **state**. It defines how the component should appear in different scenarios. \n\n### **Basic Button Story (React Example)** \n\nCreate a file **&#96;Button.stories.js&#96;** inside &#96;src/components/Button/&#96;.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from 'react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\nexport default {\n  title: 'Components/Button',\n  component: Button,\n};\n\nexport const Primary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Primary Button\" /\u003e;\nexport const Secondary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Secondary Button\" variant=\"secondary\" /\u003e;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each **export** represents a different **state of the component**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;title&#96; defines the **category in Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;component&#96; links the **UI component** to the story. \n\n---\n\n##  Using Controls for Dynamic Interaction\n\nStorybook Controls allow developers to modify props dynamically in the UI.\n\n###  Example: Adding Controls to Button\n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nexport const Playground = (args) =\u003e \u003cButton {...args} /\u003e;\n\nPlayground.args = {\n  label: 'Dynamic Button',\n  variant: 'primary',\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nNow, Storybook will provide a UI panel where developers can change **label** and **variant** dynamically.\n\n✔ Helps **test different states** without modifying the code.\n\n---\n\n##  Enhancing Storybook with Add-ons\n\nStorybook Add-ons extend functionality.\n\n###  Popular Storybook Add-ons\n\n| Add-on                     | Purpose                  |\n| -------------------------- | ------------------------ |\n| @storybook/addon-controls  | Adjust props dynamically |\n| @storybook/addon-docs      | Generate documentation   |\n| @storybook/addon-a11y      | Accessibility testing    |\n| @storybook/testing-library | UI interaction testing   |\n\n###  Installing an Add-on\n\nExample: Installing the **Accessibility Add-on**  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @storybook/addon-a11y --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; to **register the add-on**:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Adds an \"Accessibility\" panel to test contrast, ARIA attributes, and color issues.\n\n---\n\n##  Organizing Stories for Scalability\n\nA well-structured Storybook project improves maintainability. \n\n### **Recommended Folder Structure** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n📂 src\n ┣ 📂 components\n ┃ ┣ 📂 Button\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.stories.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.test.js\n ┣ 📂 .storybook\n ┃ ┣ 📜 main.js   # Configurations\n ┃ ┣ 📜 preview.js  # Global decorators\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each component has **its own folder** for easy organization.  \n  \n✔ &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; manages **configurations** and **add-ons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Automating Accessibility Testing in Storybook\n\nEnsuring your UI components are **accessible** is crucial for usability. Storybook integrates with **accessibility testing tools** to automatically detect potential issues.\n\n### **Installing the Accessibility Add-on** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-a11y\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Enabling the Add-on** \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Accessibility Tests** \n\nWhen the Storybook UI loads, a new **\"Accessibility\" panel** appears, displaying any detected issues.\n\n✔ Automatically **checks for contrast issues, missing ARIA attributes, and keyboard accessibility**.  \n  \n✔ Helps fix **WCAG compliance issues** before production. \n\n---\n\n##  Visual Regression Testing in Storybook\n\n**Visual Regression Testing** detects UI changes by comparing rendered components **before and after updates**. This ensures that UI modifications do not introduce **unintended design changes**.\n\n### **Installing Visual Testing Add-ons** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-visual-tests\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Adding a Screenshot Test** \n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { within, userEvent } from '@storybook/testing-library';\n\nexport const VisualTest = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Click me\" /\u003e;\n\nVisualTest.play = async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n  const canvas = within(canvasElement);\n  const button = canvas.getByRole('button');\n  await userEvent.click(button);\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Visual Tests** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Detects UI changes with **automatic snapshot comparisons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Mocking API Calls in Storybook\n\nStorybook can mock API requests to test UI behavior without relying on a backend.\n\n###  Example: Mocking an API Response\n\nInstall Mock Service Worker (MSW):  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install msw --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;mocks.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { setupWorker, rest } from 'msw';\n\nexport const worker = setupWorker(\n  rest.get('/api/user', (req, res, ctx) =\u003e {\n    return res(ctx.json({ name: 'Mock User' }));\n  })\n);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStart the mock server in &#96;preview.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { worker } from '../mocks';\n\nworker.start();\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Components now receive mock API responses during development.\n\n---\n\n##  Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E Testing\n\nStorybook can be used with **Playwright** to perform **end-to-end (E2E) testing** for UI components.\n\n### **Installing Playwright** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @playwright/test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Writing a Playwright Test for a Storybook Component** \n\nCreate a file &#96;Button.spec.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst { test, expect } = require('@playwright/test');\n\ntest('Check if Button component renders', async ({ page }) =\u003e {\n    await page.goto('http://localhost:6006/?path=/story/components-button--primary');\n    const button = await page.locator('button');\n    await expect(button).toHaveText('Primary Button');\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running the Playwright Test** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx playwright test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ **Combines UI component testing with full browser automation**. \n\n---\n\n##  Writing Component Tests in Storybook\n\nStorybook integrates with Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright for UI testing.\n\n###  Example: Testing with Jest + Testing Library\n\nInstall dependencies:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @testing-library/react jest --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;Button.test.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\ntest('renders the button', () =\u003e {\n  render(\u003cButton label=\"Click Me\" /\u003e);\n  expect(screen.getByText('Click Me')).toBeInTheDocument();\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Ensures components render correctly.  \n✔ Runs with npm test.\n\n---\n\n##  Deploying Storybook as Documentation\n\nStorybook can be deployed as a **component documentation site**.\n\n### **Generate Static Build** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run build-storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis creates a **&#96;storybook-static/&#96;** folder.\n\n### **Deploy to GitHub Pages** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Makes Storybook accessible via **GitHub Pages or any static host**. \n\n---\n\n##  Running Storybook in CI/CD\n\nIntegrating Storybook in CI/CD pipelines ensures UI consistency across development.\n\n###  GitHub Actions Example\n\nCreate &#96;.github/workflows/storybook.yml&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nname: Storybook CI\non: push\njobs:\n  test:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - name: Checkout Code\n        uses: actions/checkout@v2\n      - name: Install Dependencies\n        run: npm install\n      - name: Build Storybook\n        run: npm run build-storybook\n      - name: Deploy Storybook\n        run: npx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Runs Storybook on every code push.\n\n---\n\n##  Best Practices for Storybook Projects\n\n✔ **Use Controls \u0026 Docs Add-ons** for **dynamic component interaction**.  \n  \n✔ **Organize components by category** (&#96;Components/Button&#96; vs &#96;Components/Inputs&#96;).  \n  \n✔ **Automate visual \u0026 snapshot testing** to **catch unintended changes**.  \n  \n✔ **Deploy Storybook** as **live documentation** for developers \u0026 designers.  \n  \n✔ **Integrate Storybook in CI/CD** to ensure UI consistency. \n\n---\n\n## **Conclusion** \n\nStorybook is a **powerful tool for UI development, testing, and documentation**.
